articleTitle: A study on nowcasting PV generation power in a distribution network of South Korea
abstract: In recent decades, solar photovoltaic (PV) generators have been increased in a distribution network. In terms of distribution system operator (DSO), it is very important to be aware of situation of distribution network to operate the system stably and increase hosting capacity. However, most of PVs are not monitored by DSO. Thus, it is bound to be difficult to operate the system. In order to solve the problem, it is needed to nowcast(real-time estimation) generation power of non-monitored PVs. KEPCO has developed a method to nowcast PV power to monitor PVs exactly in a distribution network. This paper will introduce the nowcasting method and present a simulation results.

articleTitle: Danish electric vehicle charging profiles for distribution grid planning and design
abstract: The adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is accelerating in recent years. It is to be expected that all low power EV chargers (EVCs) will be connected to the distribution grid. The charging of EVs will considerably change the consumption patterns of residential consumers. For grid planning and design, distribution system operators need to take these new consumption patterns into consideration. This work presents a methodology to create plausible worst-case EVC profiles based on a large dataset of real charging data from 3, 547 EVCs. The resulting profiles show that EVC peak consumption presents seasonal and weekly patterns. While an aggregation of 100 EVCs has a night peak consumption of 3.5 kW per EVC on a workday in winter, in the summer it is replaced by a weekend-early-afternoon peak with a consumption of 2.5 kW per EVC. One of the main contributions of this work is the publicly available representative EVC profiles for different charger sizes, seasons, weekdays and percentiles.

articleTitle: Determination of the line parameters of electrical distribution grids based on smart meter data
abstract: Due to the decarbonization of the energy sector and the associated integration of new electrical loads and generators such as electric vehicles or PV systems, grid operators must switch to active grid operation management. This includes the control of both flexible loads and generation systems based on the knowledge of important grid parameters such as resource utilization and node voltage. Smart meters are therefore increasingly being integrated into the low-voltage level in order to determine the grid status from the recorded measurement data and the grid topology as a basis for active grid operation management. However, a current problem is that a large proportion of the line parameters, such as the line resistance, are not sufficiently digitized and in some cases incorrect, so that it is unclear at which currents line overloads occur. Within the framework of sensitivity analyses using synthetically generated smart meter data, this study investigates the influence of measurement uncertainties on the quality of the determination of the line parameters using a method based on multiple linear regression and the voltage drop along lines. This study shows that line parameter determination based on measurement data, using the here presented approach, is applicable in practice for lines with high voltage drops.

articleTitle: OPF-based determination of hosting capacity for wind power generation in high-voltage distribution grids
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method using optimal power flow (OPF) analysis to enhance distribution grid capacity for wind energy integration. Unlike conventional methods, it focuses on detailed modeling of the operational area (active and reactive power) for each wind turbine. Our OPF-based approach aims to maximize wind energy absorption by the distribution network through detailed PQ area modeling, improving grid integration accuracy. It also identifies optimal wind turbine locations within the grid, considering the impact on grid stability. The methodology accounts for uncertainties in supply tasks assessing their effects on hosting capacity and turbine placement. Simulations across different grid models validate our method’s effectiveness, demonstrating significant improvements in grid capacity for wind energy absorption and offering strategic insights for turbine placement. The results show that the positioning of wind turbines is robust against uncertainties in the supply task. Depending on the scenario, a total of 765 MW to 838 MW of additional wind power can be integrated. Furthermore, it can be concluded that the positioning of wind turbines for an exemplary grid area near the substation to the transmission grid level is advantageous.

articleTitle: Contribution to power oscillations damping of inverter based resources
abstract: This paper presents a Power Oscillation Damping (POD) controller, inspired by traditional Power System Stabilizer (PSS), as an additional control loop for Inverter Based Resources (IBRs) controlled in grid following (GFL) mode. The major idea is the contribution of several IBRs to damp electromechanical oscillations of the power system, in order to increase the power system hosting capacity. During frequency transients, the POD modifies the reactive power reference of the GFL control. The POD has the frequency measurement as input signal, and its tuning is based on the root locus design technique. This technique relies on the modal analysis, so the damping contribution is assessed through small signal stability metrics. The test case power system is a modified version of the Western System Coordinating Council (WSCC) 9-bus benchmark, which has been analysed using the DIgSILENT PowerFactory software. The results show that the proposed controller damps the electromechanical oscillatory mode in a similar way to the PSS, increasing the hosting capacity of renewables in terms of small-signal stability.

articleTitle: Graph-based modelling techniques for enhancing rural DSO digital twin frameworks: a case study from NE Spain
abstract: The energy transition poses challenges for rural Distribution System Operators (DSOs) due to increased penetration of intermittent renewable energy sources and changes in energy consumption patterns. While Digital Twin (DT) frameworks can provide the necessary tools for managing distribution grids under these uncertain conditions, their implementation generally requires extensive amounts of historic and real-time data. In this work, graph analysis tools are proposed for compartmentalizing distribution grid models. For the full graph of a grid, different sub-graph defining criteria are proposed. Using available measurements acting as border conditions, monitoring subgraphs facilitate increased load estimation accuracy and grid model validity assessment. Detected islanding conditions are also used to divide the grid in topological subgraphs. A reduced case study using a DT Framework implementation with a Spanish DSO’s ~3000 bus system shows the proposed techniques.

articleTitle: Challenges in implementing bus-section reactors to increase distribution network hosting capacity
abstract: As levels of distributed generation and storage continues to grow in distribution networks, there is key focus on increasing hosting capacity – the level of headroom available on distribution networks to connect more low carbon technologies. One aspect of hosting capacity is maximum fault level, which must be constrained below design limits to maintain a safe and secure network. The utilisation of bus-section reactors is one method of creating such headroom. This paper provides background to the technology, and explores challenges identified from system planning, operation, and network analysis. Future recommendations are made to guide the utilisation of schemes for future usage in increasing fault level capacity.

articleTitle: Demand flexibility to support probabilistic load forecasting concerns in residential scenarios
abstract: Load Forecasting usually deals with the point prediction of electricity consumption at different aggregation levels. Although the literature in this field is broad, it is quite small if we refer to the probabilistic prediction of demand, which might be particularly useful in operation and planning. In this paper, authors show some applications of probabilistic prediction in Demand Response. Quantile Regression Forest, a machine learning technique, is applied to obtain the quantiles of the conditional distribution function giving a set of probabilistic forecasts. From these predictions, demand flexibility strategies are proposed to reduce the incertitude of forecasts. Possibilities are analyzed considering Physical-Based Load Model to evaluate the potential of demand flexibility of two end-uses: Water Heating and Electric Heating. The proposal is illustrated with hourly demand data from a small Spanish city (around 5 MW of peak demand), assuming the partial control of both loads.

articleTitle: Interdisciplinary aspects of increasing the hosting capacity for photovoltaics in an Austrian context
abstract: In the context of integrating decentral renewable power generation facilities into energy systems, the term hosting capacity primarily refers to technical limitations of power grids. However, it is important to consider that technical factors are not the only barriers that may hinder the achievement of renewable expansion goals: Regulatory and economic challenges, as well as issues regarding social acceptance need to be considered accordingly. This paper provides an interdisciplinary overview of key elements that influence the achievement of national photovoltaic expansion goals in Austria. In order to create a holistic representation, multiple thematic fields are considered: technical aspects like flexibility, grid and forecasting as well as land use, social acceptance, economics and regulation. The results indicate the critical role of each thematic area. Barriers within a single field can act as bottlenecks and thus endanger the achievement of photovoltaic expansion targets. Furthermore, these thematic fields are partly interacting, which is considered in this paper as well.

articleTitle: Time series model of background voltage for hosting capacity calculations
abstract: Assessing the influence of the medium voltage (MV) network on multiple low-voltage (LV) networks in hosting capacity studies becomes important with a large share of PVs. This paper introduces the concept of background voltage to describe the impact of varying production and consumption on hosting capacity studies. A time-series model for the background voltage is presented, which considers such effects. The background voltage model has two components: the voltage drop due to consumption and the voltage rise due to PVs in other LV networks. Both components impact the hosting capacity for LV networks. Different forms of modelling these components were used to assess their impact. Using time-series for both the voltage drop and rise gives a good representation of the voltage behaviour throughout the year, creating a realistic scenario, so that different solutions can be compared towards increasing hosting capacity.

articleTitle: Risk-oriented assessment of LV distribution network hosting capacity for electric vehicles
abstract: The hosting capacity (HC) concept was initially referred only to the capacity of a distribution network (DN) to integrate distributed generation (DG) without jeopardising the correct and reliable operation of DNs. Nowadays, this concept is also extended to the capacity of integrating electric vehicle (EV) charging stations. Estimating when and how critical operating conditions can occur in the network due to the consequent increased load is necessary for Distribution System Operators (DSOs). They must find new planning solutions that consider the risk of technical constraint violations to keep it at a level set below a predefined acceptable threshold. On the other hand, looking for zero-risk planning solutions appears inadequate or too expensive in future smart and dynamic distribution scenarios. Since there is great variability in EVs and charging station specifications, EV drivers’ habits, load/generation profiles, and network data, generalisable results can arise only from a suitable probabilistic approach that can account for the relevant sources of uncertainties. In this light, this paper proposes a methodology for evaluating the EV HC of real LV DNs in different foreseen scenarios that consider the growth of demand, DERs, and charging stations simultaneously. The proposed methodology is applied to typical real LV networks, whose HC is expressed in terms of risk of technical constraint violation associated with calculated EVs’ penetration levels.

articleTitle: Accelerating rural electrification: developing innovative strategies and interventions to increase network capacity and support rural decarbonisation
abstract: The impact of increased decarbonisation of industries traditionally not associated with significant electrical energy use is of major interest for distribution network operators. Agricultural industries have historically had minimal impact on the electrical networks, whether by design or necessity. Rural networks are typified by poorer power quality and greater unreliability compared to their urban counterparts. When these industries choose to electrify raises issues for network capacity and reliability, as reinforcement or upgrade plans require development time. This paper addresses several scenarios surrounding the future of large-scale Rural Electrification efforts within the context of GB networks. Vectors of change include energy demands of developing technologies in the farming industry, practical requirements for connections of new demand and generation in rural areas and rate of uptake of new technologies. Conclusions presented within this report indicate that distribution networks operators must take the initiative to guide electrification of rural industries to manage the impact on their networks during the next two decades.

articleTitle: Enhanced coordination between transmission and distribution networks to unlock capacity for the connection of distributed generation
abstract: Within the Regional Development Programme (RDP), the UK’s first independent Distribution System Operator (DSO) of UK Power Networks (UKPN) and the Electricity System Operator (ESO) is collaborating under the Connect and Manage scheme to facilitate connections for generator customers in areas affected by transmission constraints. A significant milestone in this initiative is the introduction of the Mega Watt (MW) Dispatch Service, a market-based solution addressing pre-fault thermal constraints in the South-Eastern Power Networks (SPN). This project aims to alleviate growing regional transmission constraints by providing an alternative pathway for Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) to connect to the distribution network. This scheme has already connected 38MW of DERs and has over 1.5GW of accepted projects across the SPN region. The project's core deliverables, constituting the Minimum Viable Product (MVP), involve establishing technical dispatch solutions and contractual frameworks by collaboratively developing and integrating technical solutions (processes, data, software, and hardware systems) with industry partners. This paper aims to provide an overview of the end-to-end design of the MVP solution and Transmission-Distribution (T-D) coordination, striving for a more effective and efficient service. The solution has been successfully tested in pre-production and production environments, demonstrating its success and readiness for trial and Business As Usual (BAU) operation.

articleTitle: On the use of micro PMUs for real-time estimation of high-voltage line parameters
abstract: Accurate real-time estimation of power transmission line parameters allows to improve the performance of a range of power systems applications, such as protective relay settings, post-event fault location and power flow modelling and analysis. This paper proposes a method for real-time estimation of overhead transmission line parameters and average conductor temperature from measurements provided by micro Phase Measurement Units (μPMUs), aiming at the application on the Portuguese electrical distribution system. The developed methodology employs a linear least squares algorithm applied to the nominal pi model of an overhead high-voltage power line, and accurately estimate the line parameters. The work is conducted as a concept test, first simulated in a software only test setup using specialized computer tools, then in a real-time simulation environment with Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) to assess realμPMUs’ performance, followed by tests on a high-voltage line in the Portuguese distribution system. Real-time simulations with HILμPMUs proven to be valuable to understand the challenges of the method’s application in a controlled environment closer to a real scenario. Last, the results and challenges of accurate parameter estimation in the power distribution network are discussed.

articleTitle: Integration of heavy-duty trucks into the high-voltage grid
abstract: Current trends suggest that heavy-duty trucks will be at least partially replaced by battery-electric vehicles in the future. These vehicles place an additional burden on the electricity grid. This paper presents a method for positioning heavy-duty trucks in the power grid and determining the charging behaviour at the depot. The charging behaviour is determined by using stay profiles, which are generated by random draws based on historical mobility data. The influence of the grid integration of heavy-duty trucks on an exemplary German high-voltage grid is then analysed. This involves varying the number of heavy-duty trucks and the maximum permitted power per heavy-duty truck. The results show that the utilisation of the grid is significantly influenced by a high penetration of heavy-duty trucks. Depending on the charging strategy approach, power peaks can be prevented, thereby reducing grid utilisation.

articleTitle: Introducing the grid impact score: an indicator for DER impact on present and future grid states
abstract: With the implementation of new ambitious climate targets, e.g., FitFor55 or REPowerEU, distribution grids are experiencing a significant surge in the number of grid connection requests, primarily for Distributed Energy Resources (DER). This is especially the case at the low-voltage (LV) level. Since this unprecedented demand of requests presents substantial risks of delaying the interconnection of new DER and loads, there is an urgent need for a novel indicator providing transparency regarding the present and future states of the grid and the extent of their impact from DER integration. In this work, we introduce a novel concept, i.e., a “grid impact score”, to effectively estimate and manage the state of the grid. This grid impact score offers a comprehensive assessment of the grid safety limits and can be calculated using historical data, projected data considering future penetration rates of DER and projected data considering future penetration rates of DER combined with potential mitigation measures. We showcase the practical utility of the grid impact score when evaluating the present states of secondary substations and feeders in distribution grids, considering both European- and North American-type systems.

articleTitle: Managing prosumer exports in distribution networks through participatory export limits
abstract: This paper proposes an innovative stakeholder-centric approach for managing prosumer exports in distribution networks ensuring stakeholder benefits. The rapid inclusion of photovoltaic (PV) systems leads to excessive exports, affecting the stability and performance of the distribution networks and fostering effective export management. In addition, the emergence of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services presents challenges that may exacerbate export-related issues. Several distribution companies use fixed export limits for PV prosumers without looking at network performance. Current studies suggest dynamic limits to unlock export capabilities, providing variable export opportunities while neglecting diverse capabilities and nodal disparities of prosumers. By amalgamating dynamic export limits and prosumer priority indexing, this paper endeavours to derive individualized export limits in distribution networks. This research examined dynamic export capabilities on a real Australian suburban distribution feeder with 966 customers utilizing diverse capacities, nodal situations, and network uncertainties. The prosumer priority ranking is based on nodal constraints, time, and individual capabilities. The paper highlights participatory export limits, utilizing dynamic export limits and individual rankings, to offer enhanced export flexibility, benefiting stakeholders both distribution network operators and prosumers. These stakeholder-centric export limits provide a promising avenue for seamless PV and V2G integration toward a sustainable and resilient energy ecosystem.

articleTitle: Flexibility: bridging the gap between planning and market
abstract: The planning and operation of the distribution grid have been challenged by the high proliferation of distributed generation and the emergence of loads with new consumption dynamics. Nevertheless, these changes were accompanied by a massive deployment of metering infrastructure allowing an in-depth knowledge of load dynamics. Building on these developments, Portuguese Distribution System Operators (DSOs) has been challenged to provide alternatives to reinforcement investment consisting of market-based flexibility services. Since then, E-REDES has developed an effort, along with other stakeholders, to incorporate these alternatives into grid planning and operation and promote the development of this new market. This new paradigm involved the development of the current grid analysis tool –DPlan– to provide the flexibility service requirements for a particular grid congestion. The methodology to assess investment projects also evolved to evaluate the potential of flexibility services as a viable alternative to investment. Finally, a pilot project – FIRMe – was launched to develop internal knowledge on the subject, allowing define priorities for grid flexibility as an alternative to the investment.

articleTitle: Multi-stage optimization flexibility algorithm for demand response in ancillary services. An industrial case study
abstract: To ensure that future electrical distribution networks can effectively meet the dynamic demands of the evolving energy landscape due to the penetration of renewable energy sources, the energy-oriented industrial sector has the opportunity to enhance hosting grid capacity in response to short-term requests from system operators. This is achieved by increasing energy resources available to the grid through flexible capacity offers, aiming to prevent periods of system instability. This flexibility has traditionally been provided by large generators on the supply-side, but new opportunities for demand-side flexibility can be integrated into the industrial sector through incentive-based demand response programs. One option is to strategically allocate capacity for balancing service markets through load reduction curves. While large consumers may compete against generators in flexibility-markets, small and medium-sized industries remain largely unexplored. This paper builds on a flexible multi-single machine manufacturing problem and proposes a method for providing day-ahead demand-side flexibility offers combined with price-based real-time pricing demand response. The study is approached from the perspective of a non-intensive industry under an aggregator platform, enabling participation in balancing service auctions. The paper also examines the viability and applicability of flexibility offers within the constraints of low-capacity offers, to determine the optimal flexibility strategy.

articleTitle: Expected deviations in grid state identification through practical measurements using a smart grid interface module
abstract: One of the most important requirements for a smart grid is to know the electrical operation point, commonly referred to as the grid state. Relying purely on measurements to identify the grid state is very expensive and it is only feasible for high-voltage (HV) grids. Especially in low-voltage (LV) grids, this approach becomes economically unviable. A grid state identification, which calculates the grid state based on a selection of a few measurements and a grid model, is needed. In this paper, the effect of the number of measurements on the grid state deviation in LV grids is examined in a simulation environment. Creating a bridge between theory and practical application, this paper highlights the practical implications and expected deviations of the grid state identification using a Smart Grid Interface Module (SGIM) from BeEnergy SG GmbH in the SimBench LV grids. The findings presented herein are based on the outcomes of the mentioned simulation environment, providing insights into its effectiveness.

articleTitle: Decision support for system operators by inertia monitoring
abstract: In this paper, new system characteristics, system-operator challenges in terms of stability risks and resulting grid-calculation requirements in converter-dominated grids are summarized. A realization concept for a demonstrator is presented which allows for the system analysis and development of sophisticated decision support tools. For the relevant use case of an inertia monitoring tool, the concept is introduced taking the operators perspective into account including a discussion of relevant alternatives. Furthermore, a description of the integration of adequate concepts for the analysis of converter-dominated grids like e.g. EMT simulations is given. Resulting conditions, impediments and recommendations for system operators are discussed.

articleTitle: Optimal management of electric vehicles in a building environment: real cloud development
abstract: The increased adoption of electric Vehicles (EVs) is creating new challenges for building management. The massified use of EVs will significantly increase power consumption in buildings, potentially making it unable to answer to all encompassed loads due to insufficient available power. In the proposed paper, a pilot in the scope of the EV4EU project is described considering the management of EVs that are connected to a real building in the Azores, Portugal. Herein, a management platform is responsible for the control of two Electric Vehicles Supply Equipment (EVSEs) with Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) capability. The building also has a solar Photovoltaic (PV) system which is mainly used for self-consumption. The main results indicate that the proposed EVSE management platform successfully controls the EV charging/discharging, maximizing the state of charge of the battery through intelligent decisions based on optimization processes.

articleTitle: Assessment of the influence of renewable energy communities on future scenarios of the distribution grid
abstract: While the increasing usage of renewable energy resources is necessary, the unreliablity of these resources will have a negative impact on the energy grid. By creating financial incentives for their members renewable energy communities (RECs) may assist by consuming excess energy locally and thereby maintaining local energy balance. In this paper, the influence of renewable energy communities on the distribution grid is studied and quantified for nine different future scenarios in Austria. This is done by simulation of these nine RECs over one year. The focus is laid on photovoltaic (PV) production and the quantification of self-consumption and consumption within the REC throughout the year using dynamic partitioning. This quantification provides valuable information for the planning of a good composition of a REC, an intuitive assessment of the expected effects and a simple first estimate of suitable overall community battery sizes.

articleTitle: A cooperative game theory framework for revenues redistribution in renewable energy communities
abstract: Renewable energy communities will be able to play a key role in the energy transition to climate neutrality. The development of energy communities requires an approach that combines technical, economic, and social expertise to address the many facets; in fact, energy communities aim to improve the use of locally generated renewable energy by promoting widespread community participation, thereby fostering environmental and social sustainability. Stakeholders include citizens, government agencies, and local businesses, facilitating the sharing of local energy production, stimulating the economy through local reinvestment of revenues, and reducing emissions by shortening the electricity supply chain. Many countries in the European Union, such as Italy, have identified a system of public incentives to attract all categories of stakeholders. At this time, the equitable distribution of economic benefits poses significant challenges, and cooperative game theory approaches can provide a technical solution that can improve the interest and number of participants involved. This paper examines the application of Shapley value, with an approach derived from cooperative game theory, for equitable benefit sharing among members of an energy community. A case study designed to fit the Italian scenario is presented to validate the applicability of the methodology. The framework evaluates each member's contribution proposing a scalable model for meritocratic revenue sharing that can improve the cooperation and efficiency of internal redistribution of energy community revenues.

articleTitle: Advancing low voltage resilience: innovations in hosting capacity testing
abstract: As the world shifts towards sustainable and decentralized energy, Distribution System Operators (DSO) need versatile tools to mitigate the effects driven by the decarbonization of the energy demand. The integration of distributed energy resources (DER) and electric vehicles (EV), introduces big challenges for electrical networks. To enhance hosting capacity while preserving system stability, the distribution grid requires a structural and operational evolution for dynamic management. In this context, the UDEX Research Infrastructure, allows the exploration of hosting capacity challenges in a real-world environment. The tests detailed here primarily focus on reproducing voltage unbalance scenarios in an experimental network, with the aim to assess the efficacy of passive or active solutions in restoring balance under such conditions. In conclusion, this paper presents an investigation and real test data addressing voltage unbalances in the Low Voltage network and how to reduce them. It also outlines technical challenges and potential solutions to maximize network capacity while maintaining system stability. To navigate the Energy Transition successfully, innovation in network optimization is vital to ensure system reliability and hence specific infrastructures to test different use cases with real equipment is a valuable tool.

articleTitle: Enhancing monitoring of unobserved low voltage grids: an application case study of neural network based state estimation
abstract: It is not uncommon nowadays to find portions of low voltage distribution networks which are unobserved, meaning not monitored by the system operator. To support the growing penetration of renewable energy, proper monitoring and control of low voltage grids is essential. However, deploying a large quantity of measurement devices is not economically viable. Therefore, innovative cost-effective methods are needed to address this challenge. This paper shares the experience gained from applying a three-phase neural network-based state estimator in a real low voltage setting with limited input measurements and topology data.

articleTitle: Increasing electricity distribution network capacity on freeway stop areas to support road freight transport electrification by 2035
abstract: European and French regulations on lowering vehicle CO2 emissions are pushing road freight transport towards rapid decarbonization. This transition mainly involves the deployment of battery-electric trucks which is the main "zero-emissions vehicle" technology to be developed by truck manufacturers in the short term. The massive deployment of charging infrastructures on major roads is one of the major prerequisites for the electrification of road freight transport. The European AFIR (Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation) regulation already set targets for the deployment of such infrastructure on a large scale by 2030. Enedis, TotalEnergies, VINCI Autoroutes and six European heavy goods vehicles manufacturers have set up a working group with the aim of assessing the electric recharging needs of long-distance road freight transport on France's main roads up to 2035, and estimating the work and investment required to accommodate this new use on the transmission and distribution grids. A model of the French road network was created including main routes, origins and destinations of heavy goods vehicles journeys, and stopping areas currently used. Long-haul traffic was modelled by simulating all long-haul journeys made annually on the French road network for national and international transport, as well as international transit and cabotage. Current traffic was projected to 2035 leveraging estimated penetration rates of electric heavy goods vehicles to obtain an estimate of electric heavy goods vehicles journeys by then. Using the technological characteristics of the electric heavy goods vehicles under development and simulating driving and recharging behavior dictated by regulatory breaks, stopping times and energy required for each journey were computed. By summing up the recharging requirements for each journey, the annual recharging demand curve for each of the French road network's stopping areas were deduced at a 10-minute time step in order to estimate the energy and power needs at the French grid level. These heavy goods vehicles demand curves have been cumulated to the light vehicles demand curves estimated in a previous study. These cumulative demand curves enable ENEDIS to estimate the changes required to the electrical distribution network to accommodate vehicle recharging: construction of new source substations, reinforcement of existing medium-voltage lines.

articleTitle: Increasing distribution system hosting capacity through short-term post-fault ratings to reduce DER curtailment
abstract: The implementation of short-term post-fault ratings (STPFRs) provides a viable solution for the DNO to unlock significant latent capacity headroom, which may be used to defer Flexibility procurement and reduce additional curtailment penalties. Moreover, STPFRs have been demonstrated to provide a “little but often” benefit with significant aggregate energy volume that will further unlock latent capacity within the distribution network, enabling the DNO to consider accommodating more distributed energy resource connections, which would lead to a reduction in the overall carbon intensity of energy delivered to customers. Based on monitored data from live equipment field trials, the average potential capacity unlocked over the static post-fault rating for 50°C circuits is in the region of 0.6% and up to 1.06%, while the average potential capacity released for 75°C circuits is approximately 0.21%. This leads to a potential yearly reduction in Flexibility procurement of up to 341 MWh, equating to approximately £102,300 of financial benefit if STPFRs are adopted.

articleTitle: E-REDES solution for real-time overvoltage monitoring in LV grid | smart meter as an active asset to avoid damages and increase resilience
abstract: E-REDES has been implementing initiatives to anticipate anomalies in the low-voltage (LV) network, improve asset management efficiency, reduce outages and improve customer experience. Considering that around 75% of the occurrences with damages on customer's premises are due to grid-neutral losses, the need to detect neutral ruptures in advance and mitigate their effects was raised. In this context, a new functionality was specified for the LV smart meters to detect situations of effective neutral rupture and simultaneously disconnect customers' installations to avoid potential damage to their electrical appliances. The neutral loss detection feature is based on real-time voltage monitoring. When an overvoltage is detected the consumer's installation is disconnected from the grid through the smart meter's internal relays opening, and, as long as it remains, the smart meter does not allow the manual reconnection of the relays by the customer. This feature can also interrupt installations in an overvoltage scenario not associated with neutral loss, such as over-production. Considering the high increase of distributed generation, different voltage limits are used for injection or consumption, aiming to disconnect installations with improper injection in an overvoltage scenario, avoiding grid disturbances propagation and increasing their resilience.

articleTitle: The value of now, later, or never: assessing the value of electricity users' flexibility
abstract: The power grid faces a rising challenge of increasing variability due to the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources (RES) and the connection of more and new types of loads. This development heightens the risk of both capacity shortage and grid congestion, addressing the need to complement traditional grid extension, which is expensive and can take a long time. A promising approach is load flexibility, which is the ability of an electricity user to adjust its consumption during a set time interval. This study proposes a Flexibility Value Index (FVI) to rank electricity users based on the value of their potential flexibility. The FVI utilizes three indicators derived from a user's consumption and the local grid's load. The FVI is demonstrated on seven test profiles, followed by ranking five different types of users from Uppsala Municipality, Sweden, during winter working days. The study reveals a spread in the FVI, and the ranked list enables a public entity or a grid owner to focus resources on the users that can potentially realize the most flexibility. Furthermore, the FVI can be utilized on the production from RES, indicating which might be a suitable match to enhance the grid's hosting capacity.

articleTitle: Digitechnetz – a smart grid platform enabling an active operation of low voltage distribution grids
abstract: The energy transition has resulted in the integration of power-intensive consumers and producers into low voltage grids. This has led to an increased load on these grids, which may reach their capacity limits and thus necessitate grid expansions. However, grid expansions cannot be completed in a short-term period due to various limitations. The project DIGITECHNETZ focuses on the digital transformation of low voltage grids and proposes different use cases for an active grid management. The core component of this project is a data platform that provides essential services for active grid operation. The platform is designed with a modular and hierarchical structure to ensure interoperability and scalability. All use cases are developed and validated using Hardware-in-the-Loop tests. Subsequently, field tests are conducted to seamlessly integrate selected use cases into the operation schemes of grid operators.

articleTitle: Reactive power control strategies for renewable energy integration in MV network
abstract: The paper presents a comparative study of the potential of four reactive power management of distributed generators (DGs) for overvoltage mitigation in distribution networks. We compare a global optimisation strategy (representing a centralised reactive power management) with local reactive power management solutions. Based on the productible energy level, each strategy is assessed from a criterion of curtailed energy.

articleTitle: Inverter-based resource models for dynamic stability studies
abstract: The paper is focused on the dynamic models of inverter-based resources. The models are suitable for grid-forming inverters and applicable for stability studies of various types of resources - photovoltaics, battery systems and STATCOMs. The paper presents the models implemented in two software tools, namely MODES and EMTP. The test system refers to a medium voltage network. The transients following a transition to islanded operation are analysed considering the presence of both static loads and motors, local inverter interfaced generation and a battery storage unit. The results obtained by using the two different software tools are in close agreement.

articleTitle: Recurrent neural networks in distribution network planning: enhanced decision-making under uncertainty
abstract: The electrical distribution networks are rapidly growing due to the integration of new consumer profiles and distributed generation, creating challenges in predicting the fluctuating demand. This paper presents a distribution network planning method to address these challenges, which considers a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model, combined with a confidence interval threshold, to forecast time-series demand scenarios while considering the aggregated PV generation from smart meters. A case study in a radial medium voltage distribution network in Spain was used to test the proposed method, ensuring the operational thermal limits of transformers. This validation confirms its practical applicability in real-world scenarios, essential for maintaining network integrity and efficiency.

articleTitle: Multi-level strategy for voltage regulation in MV/LV networks
abstract: Grid evolution brings new challenges for Distribution System Operators (DSOs), such as digitalization, electrification of loads, and the increasing number of small and large power distribution sources (Distributed Energy Resources - DERs), whose rapid growth has introduced an increasing amount of non-programmable resources into the system. Moreover, the increase of the share of underground MV networks is introducing another variable: capacitive reactive power fluctuation at nighttime. Therefore, an increasing amount of network flexibility is required to maintain system stability and reliability. These challenges have led to a reconsideration of strategies to regulate voltage profile in medium and low voltage networks. Conventional voltage regulation devices in distribution networks, such as on-load tap changers (OLTCs) of transformers in HV/MV substations, voltage regulating distribution transformer (VRDTs) in MV/LV substations, line voltage regulators (LVRs) and the prosumers' inverters must be properly integrated and coordinated to obtain a supply voltage within the contractual limits. This paper proposes an innovative multi-level strategy for voltage regulation, by exploring several schemes, using cutting-edge technology for network design, operation, and control, based on the use of a multifunctional control device, sensors, and a highly reliable low-latency communication network. This results in efficient and cost-effective voltage regulation, while improving the power quality and maximizing the hosting capacity of the distribution system.

articleTitle: Impact of inverter-based distributed generation with voltage-dependent control on long-term voltage stability
abstract: This paper investigates long-term voltage stability during disturbances, considering interactions between transmission and distribution systems in the context of inverter-based distributed generation (IBDG) with voltage-dependent control. Such research is crucial for future coordination of voltage control in distribution and transmission systems and for securing long-term voltage stability. To reduce complexity, a methodology for model reduction of distribution systems with voltage-dependent control of IBDG is proposed. Such a reduction method, utilizing REI (Radial, Equivalent, Independent) grid reduction technique, may be a key for adequate representation of distributed generation and its influence on the voltage stability in the future. The validity of the method is confirmed by time domain long-term voltage simulations using detailed and reduced models. In the subsequent investigation, publicly available grid models of distribution and transmission systems are used, and the proposed reduction method is applied to distribution systems. Varying the share of IBDG with voltage-dependent control and the number of conventional power plants in the transmission system, a time-domain simulation is used to apply disturbances. The voltages in the transmission and distribution system and the influence of IBDG are observed, concluding with a discussion on the influence of distribution systems with numerous IBDG on long-term voltage stability.

articleTitle: Understanding the impact of human & corporate behaviours on DSO planning
abstract: Future flexibility markets will require the participation of new entities, like aggregators and domestic customers. The activities of these entities will have an impact on regulators' market designs as well as Distributed Network Operator (DSO) operations. Existing simulation models fall short in capturing the effects of human behaviour from domestic customers or other actors such as aggregators on the system. The paper presents PyEMLab-Agg, a new agent-based modelling tool that has been created to incorporate impacts like human behaviour, contract and risk management, as well as business model selection. According to preliminary simulations, evaluating DSO flexibility markets without taking into account consumer sentiments and social interactions may result in an over or underestimation of average market pricing of between 20% and 50%. DSO’s that use the output of such a tool could improve their ability to host additional capacity on their systems.

articleTitle: Impact of energy communities of prosumagers on quality of service in distribution network
abstract: Renewable Energy Communities (REC) can create great value and help citizens become more actively engaged in the energy transition. The paper will show how the deployment of EC of prosumagers may impact in the quality of service in distribution network and, moreover, how local flexibility involving EC can support network operations and help solving hosting capacity issues. To evaluate this impact, a low voltage distribution network was taken into consideration, consisting of 137 nodes, 135 branches, 154 users of which 15 Prosumers and 139 consumers.

articleTitle: Technology for robust, low-latency frequency and phasor estimation and evaluation with a real HV short-circuit event
abstract: With the increasing share of decentralized generation, the handling of faults requires additional attention, which is why fault-ride-through simulations are required in several countries for grid connection above a certain power. The scenarios are severe voltage dips caused by short circuits in the high-voltage grid and elimination after 60-150 ms. The aim is to prevent such an event from leading to a cascading failure of a significant proportion of decentralized generation and a subsequent imbalance between generation and consumption. Such scenarios also pose a challenge for the measurement of grid frequency, RoCoF and phasors. The assumption of a stationary behavior of the signals during the averaging interval of the measurement period is no longer valid and the results are clearly incorrect. On the one hand, such an event offers many opportunities to estimate the grid status, but no analysis is possible without reliable measurement data. On the other hand, these scenarios also often cause phase jumps in the positive sequence phasor, which leads to enormous RoCoFs and large frequency deviations in measurements based on phase-locked loops (PLL). If the behavior of an inverter, which mostly use PLLs, depends on the measured frequency, as is common in photovoltaic (PV) inverters and battery systems, a measurement error can cause a highly synchronous disturbance in a large number of inverters. In this article, we present the concept of a normalized time base with a fixed ratio to the angle of the fundamental. In this time base, the signals are periodic again and the harmonics are orthogonal again, even if the frequency of the fundamental varies. In a discrete-time implementation with interpolated sampling, this concept is applied to an in-quadrature PLL with adaptive filtering on the positive sequence phasor, but the filter can be optimally and robustly designed and rigidly implemented in the normalized time base. In an FPGA-based implementation, the phasors and the frequency are calculated 16 times per line cycle and are therefore available approx. 800 times per second. The runtime of < 30ms is very short and is suitable for the realization of virtual rotating masses. In our laboratory, a real live event similar to the simulation of a fault ride through was measured on low-voltage lines. The event occurred twice with an interval of a few tens of seconds. Therefore, it was identified as a high-voltage short-circuit event (most likely on a 110 kV line). We will present the measurement results of one of these events. With the help of background knowledge about the behavior of grids and protection devices, the result could be corrected. Based on these corrected results, the behavior of the systems and the requirements for the measurements will be discussed.

articleTitle: Implementing a real option valuation method to analyse electricity network infrastructure investments with uncertainties
abstract: There is an increasing need for investments in the electricity distribution network due to the on-going clean energy transition. At the same time, distribution system operators (DSOs) are facing more uncertainties regarding their planned investments. Traditional investment analyses may not comprehensively take into account the future uncertainties and may ignore the possibilities that would have an impact on the investments. Their ability to capture managerial flexibility in adapting to unexpected market developments is limited. In the paper, we study the feasibility of implementing real option valuation methodology to investment analysis of a distribution system operator. In particular, the benefits of real option theory over traditional investment analysis methods are investigated in this context. The feasibility study of the chosen real option method was implemented in a Finnish DSO Helen Electricity Network Ltd (Helen DSO). The results demonstrate that real options valuation gives a new additional approach to analyse electricity network investments with uncertainties.

articleTitle: Adaptability of models and resilience of electricity forecasts on Enedis’ distribution network in response to new phenomena and changing behaviours regarding energy consumption
abstract: In order to anticipate congestion and enable the activation of levers ensuring electricity supply quality and network safety, grid operation activities within Enedis rely on energy forecasts. In recent years, new phenomena and changes in behaviour regarding energy consumption have modified electricity consumption profiles, requiring Enedis to increase the speed at which its forecasting models adapt. Following lockdowns and curfews during the Covid-19 pandemic, the rise in energy prices and incentives promoting energy sobriety linked to the Russo-Ukrainian War rapidly led to a 7% to 15% drop in electricity consumption at the local level. The decision to turn off hot water tank engagements to facilitate the heating period also drastically modified the intra-day consumption profiles by shifting the peaks. In order to be more resilient towards future phenomena whose consequences are not yet observable, Enedis developed new short-term adjustment techniques using past data. These techniques are not specific to past observed phenomena, allowing the rapid adaptation of forecasting Machine Learning models to future behaviours. This article provides insights on the models used and the resulting effects in terms of forecast quality, adaptability and control of the operational and financial risks of the distribution network.

articleTitle: Demonstrating the effectiveness of active voltage control technologies in congested low-voltage distribution networks
abstract: The electricity network consists of high-voltage transmission and medium- to low-voltage (LV) distribution systems. Transmission is looped and easily controlled, while distribution is radial, vulnerable to outages, and lacks remote operation capability except for limited interventions. Real-time data from distribution is rare. Traditional grid design was functionally adequate until the rise of many solar and small power plants. To meet climate goals, the network must accommodate renewable energy production, requiring adjustments beyond voltage drop considerations to handle voltage fluctuations. As part of an innovation project, a Hungarian DSO has installed in-line voltage regulator (IVR) and on-load tap changer transformer (OLTC) units in more than 20 LV network locations, with the aim to demonstrate their effectiveness in voltage control. During the pilot, a measurement campaign was also conducted to properly assess the effects of these units on power quality and the fluctuation of the voltages. In our paper the detailed results of these pilots are presented, focusing not only on the numerical results concerning the decrease of voltage variations, but also providing insight to operational experiences. Finally, the best practices are presented on how the LV supply areas should be selected to maximise the technical capabilities of IVR and OLTC units.

articleTitle: Electric mobility: analyzing the role of battery swap stations in addressing range anxiety and grid impact
abstract: Over the past decade, addressing Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions has become crucial, with the transport sector being a major contributor due to fossil fuel reliance, particularly in urban areas. In response, European countries are promoting a shift to greener alternatives, focusing on Electric Vehicles (EVs) and developing necessary infrastructure. Battery Swap Stations (BSS) provide an innovative solution for addressing concerns linked to conventional charging infrastructure. This includes reducing charging times and mitigating range anxiety. Furthermore, BSSs effectively handle and store battery packs, optimizing energy utilization and improving grid stability via bidirectional interaction with the electrical grid. The installation of a BSS in an Low Voltage (LV) feeder increases the host capacity by introducing a flexible load capable of absorbing power if requested and possibly inverting the power flow. This study aims to offer a comprehensive insight into how BSSs facilitate the transition to electric mobility, addressing user apprehensions and promoting environmentally-friendly urban transport infrastructure while bolstering grid capabilities. This paper assesses the effects of BSSs on reducing range anxiety, enhancing EV user satisfaction, and improving local grid stability and hosting capacity. The first part offers a vision of this new technology, followed by an analysis of the impacts that the introduction of BSS may have on an electric car-sharing fleet and their impact on the grid.

articleTitle: Extending voltage thresholds in MV grids to increase hosting capacity
abstract: The largest French DSO Enedis is developing a new voltage management scheme to improve the integration of a massive number of distributed generators (DG) as well as end-use electrification evolutions, by optimizing voltage thresholds for transformers, MV feeders and LV grids in network development. Current grid-planning rules for allocating voltage margins from the primary substation to the different types of customers are inherited from a period when the main voltage concern was to prevent voltage drops. The objective of this new voltage scheme is to reduce grid investment costs and to increase the hosting capacity of French MV grids for DG. Implications of this new method are illustrated through a real-life case study in which both “high generation” and “high load” network sizing reference situations are simulated. This new voltage scheme is valued in relation to the net present value of investments required to guarantee an adequate power supply quality.

articleTitle: Electric vehicle charging stations support in unintentionally islanded distribution system
abstract: The paper deals with the support of EV charging stations in distribution system being subjected to the unintentional islanding, i.e. separation from the rest of the interconnected power system. Dynamic simulations on a simplified model of the HV distribution system are used to assess the potential of charging stations, considering different types of their support. The distribution system model consist of a local heating power plant, photovoltaics, charging stations and heat pumps. The results being discussed clearly show the benefits of grid support from charging stations. However, the technical and legislative support will be needed to exploit them in the future. In addition, the dynamic model can be modified for analysis of the support in another (specific) distribution system.

articleTitle: Methodology to increase hosting capacity through voltage control of distribution network based on technical requirements of smart inverter
abstract: Increasing continuously renewable energy reduces system robustness and causes supply and demand problems in the event of serious system faults. Accordingly, domestic, and foreign power utilities are establishing and operating grid connection regulations for renewable energy, and technical requirements are becoming more diverse as the system changes. Additionally, methodology is needed to improve the flexibility of distribution networks and hosting capacity of renewable energy based on technical requirements. Therefore, in this paper, we define the technical requirements of smart inverters as below and analyze their necessity in situations of voltage violations due to system faults. In addition, we propose a method to improve the hosting capacity of renewable energy through voltage control of smart inverters for restoration of the distribution network. The voltage control algorithm of smart inverters is implemented using MATLAB-Simulink as below, and the VRT (Voltage Ride Through) model for technical requirements is also implemented. Using this model, we simulate the voltage violation scenarios for faults and analyze the impact on distribution network recovery according to the characteristics of smart inverters.

articleTitle: Assessing utilities business models based on the economic benefits of including NWA in distribution planning
abstract: Planning studies evaluate the technical and economic viability of project alternatives to maintain and expand the power grid by sorting them out based ontheir economic cost within a time frame, aiming to distinguish projects that fit better with the utility’s priorities. This comparison reveals the advantages and disadvantages of each alternative, depicting the business model advancements needed for taking them to reality. This paper presents a utility planning study developed using EPRI’s Automated Distribution Assessment & Planning Tools (ADAPT), which generated multiple project alternatives for the utility on a 9-year time frame. These alternatives are evaluated technically and economically in ADAPT to sort them out revealing the most cost-effective, presenting to the planner the benefits and drawbacks of the technologies used for each project. Based on these results, we will discuss the impact on the business model and the organizational challengesfor implementing 5 of the projects identified through ADAPT as the most cost-effective. This discussion includes the inclusion of new technologies in the utility’s service portfolio, their impact on the long-term system performance regarding other technical goals such as reliability and resilience, and the benefits for the business regarding investment deferrals when combining traditional and NWA mitigation alternatives.

articleTitle: Research on the impact of superconducting cables on the urban power grid capacity
abstract: With the rapid growth of the power load in the urban centre, the expansion of power capacity by constructing conventional cables is not always feasible due to the limited underground passageways. The superconducting cable, possessed with features of zero resistance, large current-carrying capacity and small size has become an excellent solution to this problem. According to the cable characteristics, the fault of superconducting cable generally develops slowly. Besides, the carrying capacity of superconducting cable can be increased with the decrease of temperature and can achieve short-term overload under lower temperature conditions. Therefore, the application of superconducting cable essentially improves the safety of power grid equipment. According to the power supply, one superconducting cable can replace four to six conventional cables with same cross section and voltage level, and multiple switch stations in the central urban area can be merged into one switch station, which not only reduces the space demand for the central urban area, but also improves the construction feasibility of power supply facilities, and increases the flexibility and reliability of the power grid operation mode.

articleTitle: Hosting capacity of meshed distribution grids with and without smart solutions
abstract: Alternative solutions, instead of building new transmission lines, are needed to enable the fast electrification of sectors such as industry, transportation, and heating. This includes smart-grid technology allowing for an increase in hosting capacity without the need for building new transmission lines. The increase in hosting capacity beyond the firm hosting capacity is, with many of the schemes, related to the ability of the installation to tolerate curtailment. The paper gives an overview of different smart-grid schemes and how they potentially increase the hosting capacity. The connection of a large electrolyser installation for hydrogen production is used as an illustrative example introducing some of the issues.

articleTitle: Stochastic analysis-based assessment for PV hosting capacity considering energy storage systems and dynamic voltage control device in a distribution feeder
abstract: Solar PV generation is widespread in the distribution system nowadays, and high-penetration PV brings challenges to reliable grid operation. Taiwan’s government has set a policy goal of achieving 20% of total electricity generation from renewable sources by 2025. However, the intermittent and unpredictable nature of renewable energy leads to voltage deviation and overvoltage in distribution system buses. Nevertheless, increasing PV capacity in distribution feeders is crucial to achieving the 2025 target. This study employs a stochastic analysis method to simulate PV hosting capacity accommodated in a distribution feeder. The study incorporates dynamic reactive power compensation devices for distribution feeders to assess the maximum hosting capacity of PV, in addition to smart inverters and energy storage systems (ESSs). Simulations are performed using OpenDSS with Matlab for power flow calculations and result analysis. The results show that the proposed method is effective for assessing PV hosting capacity in a distribution feeder.

articleTitle: System strength monitoring: definition, metrics and use cases applied to modern system operation
abstract: In systems with high penetration of Inverter Based Resources (IBRs), ensuring the stability and reliability of power systems is paramount. This paper delves into the critical area of power system stability, emphasizing the understanding and measurement of system strength. We first present a comprehensive literature review of system strength definitions and metrics. Then, an innovative methodology for real-time monitoring of system strength metrics is presented. We will finally investigate how this innovative system strength measurement solution may help the stable and efficient operation of real-life power systems. With a focus on addressing challenges arising from the transition to IBRs, the paper advocates for measurement-based system strength monitoring. Proactive identification of challenges, real-time assessment, and incorporation of system strength metrics into operational planning emerge as key strategies for optimizing grid stability and reliability.

articleTitle: Evaluation of the flexibility provision behaviour of different charging strategies for electric vehicles
abstract: Electric vehicle charging offers great potential for providing flexibility in the electric power grid by acting as mobile energy storage and providing both uni- and bidirectional flexibility. So far, various simulation methods have been developed to estimate the flexibility potential, but these are often based on theoretical assumptions and refer to an optimal charging behaviour of EVs. This assumption, however, is not always valid. Considering real-world behaviour, which depends on the EV type is, therefore, essential for future simulation and evaluation of EV-flexibility provision. Within this work, issues such as the reliability of charging/discharging processes, response times, efficiency levels, minimum possible charging power, plausibility of the ISO 15118 parameters and different charging profiles are examined in detail. Different vehicle models are tested regarding their ability to provide flexibility, taking into account various charging and discharging scenarios. The results are then verified with external measurements. It could be shown that the behaviour of vehicles from different manufacturers differ in their inherent charging behaviour, which can be significant for reliability of flexibility provision, since the realization of predefined charging profiles is not always possible. Furthermore, the realization of predefined charging profiles is not always possible. The ISO 15118 partially transmits incorrect parameters. Hence, the provision of flexibility within a field-test faces several challenges, that has to be considered in the estimation and activation of flexibility potential.

articleTitle: Techno-economics evaluation of electrolyser technologies: multicriteria decision making with SmartGridEval
abstract: The global landscape of hydrogen use has witnessed significant developments. Its high energy density and ability to be stored for an extended period make it an excellent fuel for storage systems. Green hydrogen, produced through renewable electricity, is identified as a crucial complement to optimising renewable energy production via the electrolysis process and provides several benefits to the power system, including avoiding network criticalities (e.g., overvoltages and overcurrents), using the excess energy during renewable energy sources peak generation time, enhanced distribution network hosting capacity, increased system flexibility, and improved system efficiency. The technology for producing green hydrogen includes different electrolysers, such as alkaline, polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM), anion exchange membrane (AEM), etc. In this paper, the appraisal of the most suitable electrolyser technology will be identified through Multi-Criteria Analysis (MCA) and Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) using the ISGAN SmartGridEval. The paper explores the techno-economic analysis and comparison of various key performance indicators (KPIs), such as electrolyser efficiency, electrolyser capacity, hydrogen production rate through the HySupply tool, and cost-effectiveness (operational cost, capital cost), to identify the best technology that can increase green hydrogen production by using variable RES fluctuations and analyse its impact on the hosting capacity of the power sector.

articleTitle: Implementation of a technical solution for the grid-friendly control of flexible loads
abstract: In this paper, a methodology to control flexible loads for grid friendly usage is presented. We demonstrate the methodology with a pilot installation (minimum viable product – MVP), in which an existing electric vehicle charging infrastructure is used. The infrastructure is connected to a control-device using relay contacts which receives commands to reduce the load from our flexibility platform whenever a bottleneck in the grid is detected. In our pilot installation, we demonstrate how the end-to-end process works, i.e. from running a load flow analysis and detecting a bottleneck to sending the command to the control-device that effectively reduces the load. Furthermore, we present the key challenges that we have encountered during development and implementation, and we present our recommendations from a DSOs point of view for future flexibilities. The presented methodology has the potential to increase the hosting capacity of the grid, especially with regards to the increase of the number of heat-pumps, electric vehicles and photovoltaic installations.

articleTitle: SysZell: a holistic approach for providing ancillary services in cellular energy systems
abstract: The shift towards more renewable generation, the decline of thermal power plants and increased demand from electric vehicles and heat pumps challenges the electricity system operation. TheSysZellproject focuses on ancillary services for frequency stabilization in an altered institutional setup. It builds on the Cellular Energy System concept proposed in the projectZellNetz2050which co-optimizes power scheduling and transmission in a decentralized manner. This setup mitigates grid overloading and minimizes short-term interventions. However, ancillary service provision has not been addressed so far. In expectation on how network frequency stabilization will change in the future, this projects assesses how the previous works can be extended. This contribution highlights the research project’s content, notably analyses of alternatives for procurement of frequency stability services, application of simulations, and designing decision-support tools.

articleTitle: Gradient projection-based online feedback optimisation for distribution grid management
abstract: The increasing use of renewable energy sources within distribution grids has raised concerns about grid stability, power quality, and congestion. Especially, the share of energy generated by photovoltaics has grown considerably. However, the optimal use of their inverters has also been proposed as a possible solution to mitigate such concerns through reactive power compensation and curtailment. This paper introduces several optimisation algorithms for online feedback optimisation and states their advantages and disadvantages. A projected gradient descent algorithm is developed and tested under practical considerations such as com- munication delays, measurement errors, and modelling inaccuracies in the form of Gaussian noise. Simulations were performed on a medium voltage distribution grid model using exact AC power flow. The findings suggest that the algorithm is robust to measurement noise and modelling errors but it is susceptible to communication delays.

articleTitle: A monitoring and control architecture to increase the hosting capacity in non-synchronous distribution systems
abstract: The ever-growing and decentralized production from Renewable Energy Sources (RES) has altered the traditional paradigm where electrical distribution systems were conceived for unidirectional flows of energy from higher to lower voltage levels. This transformation raises concerns about several planning and operational aspects, especially in non-synchronous power systems. Such electrical networks are more susceptible to face instability conditions due to the stochastic and intermittent nature of RES, and their inability to provide physical inertia and sustain voltage levels in case of disruptive events. For these reasons and for the low level of smartization of such electrical networks, the hosting capacity is relatively low and the RES penetration is often limited in favour of thermal generation. Clearly, by limiting the hosting capacity of such networks, some of the advantages arising from higher RES integration come less. This paper presents a hierarchical architecture for the monitoring and control of non-synchronous distribution systems, which aims to enable isolated power systems to accommodate a larger amount of RES while preserving their reliability. The control scheme is the result of the collaboration between e-distribuzione, Gridspertise and Politecnico di Bari in the framework of the Italian research project ISMI.

articleTitle: Methods and techniques used to produce electricity forecasts on Enedis’ distribution network at a finer grid than the HV/MV substation
abstract: Since 2015 Enedis has been producing and using electricity consumption and generation forecasts for all 2,300 HV/MV substations. However, the increasing integration of renewable energies on the MV and LV networks and the decision to smooth out generation peaks under normal operating conditions have increased the complexity of Enedis’ flows. To ensure the quality of its supply and electrical safety, Enedis now needs a finer geographic grid modelling to anticipate and handle potential constraints, such as congestion or high voltages. To meet this challenge, Enedis developed an innovative technical approach enabling robust and reliable forecasting at increasingly finer grids, including the 750,000 MV/LV substations. This approach combines dimension reduction for energy modelling and massive parallelization of calculations for calibration and forecasting stages. Generating forecasts at these finer grids significantly increased the volume of data generated, stored and transmitted to various stakeholders in the electricity system. Enedis met this challenge by redesigning the architecture of its database using Big Data tools.

articleTitle: Evaluation of business models to enable integrated local energy community use cases and provide customer value
abstract: The eNeuron project aims to develop a pioneering toolbox framework for the optimal design and operation of multi-carrier energy systems, such as integrated local energy communities based on the energy hub concept. In today's rapidly evolving business and regulatory landscape, the evaluation of business models has become a critical endeavor for stakeholders aiming to remain competitive and maximise their revenues. With the advent of technological advancements and changing customer expectations, stakeholders must continuously assess and adapt their business models to enable effective use cases. Business model evaluation serves as a strategic tool that can enable businesses to identify strengths and weaknesses, assess market viability, and capitalise on emerging opportunities. By comprehensively analysing and refining their business models, stakeholders can optimise their operations, drive innovation, and ultimately achieve sustainable success in an increasingly dynamic and interconnected world. This paper provides an overview of the approach developed and the steps that were carried out as part of the eNeuron project to develop and evaluate business models to facilitate the implementation of local energy community use cases. Examples of developed business models included local flexibility, co-operative heating, peak shifting, and hydrogen-based storage.

articleTitle: Probabilistic adoption scenarios of distributed energy resources in residential buildings for a geospatial projection of the electrical load
abstract: This paper presents a method that assesses the likelihood of building-level Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) adoption, factoring in the influence of other pre-installed DER technologies. Utilizing a case study in Hamburg, Germany, we estimate the adoption likelihood of Air-Source Heat Pumps (ASHP) in residential buildings, considering the influence of already installed Photovoltaic (PV) systems. The results uncover the expected ASHP adoption pattern in Hamburg, highlighting the spatial variations in adoption rates, particularly between urban and rural settings. The results also highlight the varying impact of PV on ASHP adoption. They illustrate how the presence of PV systems may affect the adoption likelihood of ASHP, depending on building features such as type or current heating system. Our case study methodology effectively uses data insights to identify potential DER growth areas, critical for grid operators in enhancing hosting capacity. Specifically, by identifying flexibilities, operators can maximize hosting capacity without expanding the grid. When expansion is necessary, understanding future load distributions enables more informed infrastructure investment. The comprehensive approach, as exemplified in our Hamburg case study, follows a generic framework, which can be used for similar analyses in other regions or with other technologies.

articleTitle: Optimizing solar panel integration in low voltage networks: utilizing short-circuit current and Q(V)-characteristics
abstract: In low voltage networks, distributed generation poses significant challenges due to voltage rise and rapid voltage change. In low voltage networks, there can be low short-circuit currents at the connection point. This study investigates the method of using the short-circuit current at the connection point to estimate the maximum generation before the maximum voltage level and rapid voltage change is violated. The new EN 50549-1 standard and Finnish Energy recommendation ofQ(V)-characteristics are investigated to estimate their role in increasing the amount of allowed generation at the connection point characterized by the short-circuit current. As a result, we obtain curves for the allowable amount of generation of the inverter as a function of short-circuit currents. The findings will determine the maximum solar panel size for a single connection point before its self- induced voltage rise or rapid voltage change is violating standards and recommendations. This method can relax overly restricting rules that may limit the present allowed solar panel generation at the customers’ premises and withdraw non-necessary network upgrades and delays when deploying distributed solar generation. This way the study seeks to promote faster renewable energy growth, thus contributing to a more sustainable energy future.

articleTitle: UK-based local flexibility trials: lessons from ADEPT, LEO & SCOTCLUE
abstract: Distribution System Operators (DSOs) and Municipal Authorities across various local energy flexibility trials, are encountering challenges and opportunities within their innovation projects.
