This paper aims to present common challenges and share insights gained from a comparative study of local energy flexibility trials in the UK, contributing to the advancement of smart local energy systems outlined in the EU Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) directive.This paper presents case studies and learning from each of the following projects, outlining a strategy for establishing more RECs:<list list-type="bullet" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><list-item> <label>•</label> The Association of Directors for Environment Planning and Transport (ADEPT) Live Lab is an innovation project which focused on municipal decarbonisation and transport opportunities including the monitoring and visualisation of renewable energy assets installed within municipal buildings. </list-item> <list-item> <label>•</label> The Local Energy Oxfordshire (LEO) project trials deliver key learnings on distribution control architectures for providing local flexibility to DSOs as well as exploring services such as peer-to-peer trading. </list-item> <list-item> <label>•</label> The CLUE (Concepts, Planning, Demonstration and Replication of Local User-friendly Energy Communities) project is a demonstration that validates a Web of Cells (WoC) distribution control approach through the delivery of a Vector Integration Platform (VIP) for control and monitoring applications. </list-item> </list>

articleTitle: Unlocking commoditised local demand-side flexibility through a structured and competitive market, based on the universal smart energy framework (USEF): learnings from an innovation trial in Scotland
abstract: Local demand-side flexibility offers a cost-effective alternative to traditional grid reinforcement; however, participation remains in its infancy with its full potential yet to be unlocked. In particular, residential flexibility remains a vast and largely untapped resource. The innovative FUSION project investigated how to encourage flexibility from industrial, commercial and residential consumers with access to a broad spectrum of flexible assets connected to low voltage network. FUSION trialled commoditised local demand-side flexibility through a structured and competitive market, based on the Universal Smart Energy Framework (USEF) over an 18-month period. This paper discusses practical experience with flexibility markets, interaction with customers as well as the customer and aggregator experience with USEF innovative elements; a market coordination mechanism for standardising trading, a trading protocol for communication and data exchange between market participants, and the concept of 'free bids' enabling ad-hoc bidding outside of contractual arrangements. It also analyses the impact of baselining performance on the DSO and flexibility providers, as well the key DSO flexibility procurement cost drivers.

articleTitle: Real time fault level monitoring to increase electricity distribution network utilisation
abstract: A novel Real Time Fault Level Monitor device has now been fully developed and commissioned within a UK electricity distribution network. Fault level – the worst-case electrical current that will flow through a network in the event of a fault – is becoming a greater challenge to manage due to increasing energy demands and changing profiles for electricity generation, making the need for accurate fault level data essential. For the first time, continuous monitoring data has been obtained that demonstrates network fault level as a dynamic value, with daily, weekly or even hourly fluctuations evident in the data. This opens possibilities for new ways of planning and operating networks to maximise network utilisation, accommodating the influx of distributed renewable generation and to facilitate the Net Zero transition.

articleTitle: Peak load estimation based on consumer heating type classification powered by deep learning
abstract: The heating system of a building could significantly impact the aggregated electricity peak load. It is in the interest of the distribution system operators (DSOs) to both know what type of heating system that is connected to the grid, and the impact of end-users changing their heating system. Focusing on the transition from non-electric heating systems to heat pumps, this paper investigates its impact on peak load consumption. A state-of-the-art heating type classification method using smart meter data and deep learning was used to to first classify the heating types of single-family dwellings. Building upon previous work, a multi- label approach was adopted with the classifier to accommodate buildings with multiple heating sources. To assess the impact of heating system changes, smart meter data were substituted with data from similar buildings equipped with heat pumps. This process was repeated for statistical confidence. A geographical analyses identify areas susceptible to a large peak load increase, demonstrating practical application.

articleTitle: Towards a successful implementation of advanced distribution management systems (ADMS) for grid modernisation
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive guide based on DNV NextGen GridOps framework in implementing an Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) as part of utilities’ grid modernisation initiative. By aligning project objectives with the organisation’s strategic vision, utilities can unlock the full potential of ADMS capabilities and drive a smarter, more resilient energy future. This guide emphasises critical aspects such as architecture, data management, integration, technical considerations, and fostering cross-functional teams. Utilities can leverage this guide to embark on their ADMS journey, to achieve fast and successful implementation.

articleTitle: Electric vehicles in an Alpine distribution grid: impact assessment and mitigation through smart charging
abstract: The increasing uptake of electric vehicles (EVs) foreseen threatens the stability of both medium (MV) and low-voltage (LV) distribution networks. Specifically, MV/LV transformers will experience high loading periods due to the residential EV chargers drawing power in the early evening or public chargers being used during the day and night, depending on the parking regulations. In this work, we present the future impact of EV charging on the distribution grid of the city of Trento, Italy. Firstly, a detailed power grid model was developed and validated using the measured data collected in the primary substations; then the analysis of the impact of different EV mass penetration scenarios on the MV/LV transformers was performed via power flow simulations. The results show that for EV penetration levels lower than 50%, the transformers are not heavily impacted until 2050, but if the number of EVs increases to "rapid" penetration scenarios, the violation frequency in urban transformers increases by 13.5% compared to the previous one, and additional undervoltage events could be experienced at the LV side. Finally, we evaluated the effect of a centralised smart EV charging strategy, including Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capabilities, and the results show that it minimises the transformer overloading frequency values.

articleTitle: Local flexibility approach from ENEDIS, E-DISTRIBUZIONE, and E-REDES to boost grid hosting capacity
abstract: The transition from fossil fuels to renewables in the energy industry driven by carbon neutrality goals and the growing adoption of distributed energy resources, like solar panels and wind turbines, is reshaping the traditional dynamics of the energy sector. DSOs must address challenges arising from the variability of renewable sources, evolving demand patterns, and the need for resilient solutions. In this dynamic context, flexibility solutions emerge as a complement to optimise network reinforcement plans. These solutions play a pivotal role in supporting distribution system hosting capacity during emergencies or while network reinforcement is undergoing, equipping operators with the tools and mechanisms necessary to surmount challenges and leverage opportunities arising from the evolving energy sector trends. Considering the regulatory framework is not completely defined at the country level, this paper aims to share ENEDIS, E-DISTRIBUZIONE and E-REDES practical experiences in flexibility solutions. Therefore, this paper will contribute to the dissemination of valuable knowledge and practical insights into flexibility solutions; sharing the results of each country's tenders for flexibility service acquisition can guide and inspire other DSOs, researchers, and policymakers seeking flexibility solutions and provide a reference point for best practices in developing local, flexible markets.

articleTitle: Research on distributed PV consumption control method
abstract: The traditional distribution network has been developed into a new distribution network with multi-power supply, bidirectional power current and a large number of new power electronic equipment access, after large number of distributed resources such as photovoltaic, wind power and energy storage are connected to the medium and low voltage distribution system. The active power of distributed generators such as photovoltaic wind generators is greatly affected by meteorological factors and has strong randomness and volatility, which brings difficulties for the safe and stable operation control of the active distribution networks. Sometimes photovoltaic or wind generators have to be decreased output or even given up, which reduces the economy incomes of DGs’ owners and reliability of distribution system. To solve this problem, an operational control method has been proposed to improve the load-bearing capacity of the distribution system in this paper . The method aims to maximize the consumption ability of distributed generators, and establishes an active power coordination control model for distribution system meeting with the safe operation constraint. This model has the characteristics of multi spatiotemporal comprehensive optimization and it is a multidimensional comprehensive optimization method. In terms of time dimension, it is divided into day-ahead strategy optimization, intraday ultra short-term strategy optimization, and real-time control optimization. In terms of space dimension, it is divided into three levels: regional autonomy, inter regions collaboration, and global optimization. The specific implementation method is as follows: regional autonomy includes coordinated control of distributed energy sources such as photovoltaic generators, wind power generators, and energy storage systems within one MV/LV transformer supplying area to achieve power autonomy within the MV/LV transformer supplying area, flexible interconnection of the low-voltage areas power supplied by the distribution transformers within one MV feeder to achieve flexible mutual power exchanging within the MV transformers, and coordinated control of distributed energy sources within the feeder supply area to achieve the feeder autonomy. Inter regional collaboration refers to the power balance and collaboration among various feeders within the scope of the group of feeders tied, which is achieved through network reconfiguration and coordinated control of distributed energy sources . Global optimization realizes the DERs’ daily output planning and real-time output adjustments for the distribution system, and sends them to the corresponding control center. Theoretical analysis and simulation examples show that the operation control method of the distribution system can reduce the DGs’ power discarded rate of the distribution system, and can improve the power consumption ability of DG, and can improve the load bearing capacity of the distribution system. The method is easy to implement and has broad application prospects in real distribution automation systems.

articleTitle: E-REDES grid flexible power solution for EV charging at residential buildings
abstract: The transition to cleaner energy and the electrification of transport has led to a significant increase in electric vehicles (EVs). Accordingly, the increasing penetration of EVs has created a demand for an expanded network of public and private EV charging stations (EVCS). This demand requires an investment in charging infrastructure and the reinforcement of the low-voltage distribution grid to meet the power demand requirements. Increasing the power capacity of the distribution grid is costly and sometimes time-consuming. Therefore, it is crucial to find solutions that can accelerate the installation of EV charging stations by using the power currently available in the grid. E-REDES has been actively developing solutions to stimulate and facilitate the installation of electric vehicle charging stations through flexible power solutions. A notable example is the FlexConnection project, which implements a flexible power management solution for EV charging in collective buildings with garages/boxes powered by a common services circuit. This flexible solution increases the power capacity of the host distribution grid. It allows more EV charging stations to be installed within the building's common services circuit, facilitating flexible EV charging without exceeding the building's maximum power limit or requiring an increase in the power capacity of the distribution grid.

articleTitle: Deep reinforcement learning-based operation strategy for high resilience distribution system
abstract: With the escalating frequency and severity of natural disasters due to global warming, ensuring stable power supply to critical infrastructure like fire stations, hospitals, and communication facilities becomes imperative for urban recovery and social safety. Previous studies have focused on various approaches for continuously operating power grids, often employing optimisation models. However, these models suffer from high computation times, necessitating a prompt approach to handling unexpected events. Machine learning (ML)-based algorithms offer a solution by pre-training parameters and swiftly determining control signals based on different scenarios. Among ML techniques, reinforcement learning (RL) learns through experience and rewards, akin to the objective function in optimisation. The resilience evaluation is validated through natural disaster simulations in the IEEE 123-node test feeder. Moreover, an optimal operation model based on deep-RL (DRL) is developed to utilise renewable energy resources (RES) and energy storage systems (ESS) effectively in distribution systems, and to ensure uninterrupted power supply to critical loads. Specifically, the model addresses natural disaster scenarios, maximising the use of DER and ESS while maintaining power balance.

articleTitle: TSO/DSO coordination for generation management in Portugal
abstract: The integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid has heightened variability and uncertainty in power generation, challenging Distribution System Operators (DSOs) and Transmission System Operators (TSOs) in effective grid management. Coordinated generation management between DSOs and TSOs is vital to enhance grid capacity for new generation, ensuring stability and reliability while accommodating renewable sources. This coordination prevents distribution grid constraints, maintaining balance requirements. Coordinated management is crucial for flexible generation connected to the distribution grid, where limitations must be occasionally imposed to safeguard grid integrity. The Portuguese TSO (REN) and DSO (E-REDES) collaborated closely, establishing a coordination agreement thus creating the conditions for flexible generation connection to grid. Using existing market tools and regulations, the agreement enables TSO to relay market information to DSO, informing about constraints, and vice versa. Market operations include Day Ahead, Intraday, and Ancillary Markets organised by TSO, crucial for system balancing. Emergency procedures for unexpected constraints ensure swift response through real-time communication between operators, activating necessary compensation measures promptly. The authors assert this approach fosters effective generation management, utilising existing market tools while minimising Distributed Energy Resources (DER) requirements.

articleTitle: Innovative toolbox for distribution grid planning and design for enhanced hosting capacity
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy and electrification of demand lead to substantial challenges for distribution grids. This, coupled with the need to increase the installed renewable capacity implies costly investments to reinforce the distribution grid. Within this scenario, the use of new grid services, such as storage or flexibility services becomes relevant to maintain the safe system operation and enhanced hosting capacity, while at lower costs. This work presents the results of the research conducted within the Beyond H2020 and DataCellar HE projects where a holistic toolbox for Distribution System Operator (DSO) is developed, intending to facilitate network planning by using new resources to maintain the grid parameters in situations with high Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) penetration.

articleTitle: E-REDES flexibility strategy to enhance distribution system hosting capacity
abstract: The energy sector is undergoing a paradigm shift driven by forces such as the increasing integration of distributed renewable generation and the electrification of consumption. Therefore, to effectively manage the challenges posed by these macro trends, DSOs need to implement innovative solutions for grid management, including enhancing grid flexibility. In this context, this paper explores the flexibility strategy to enhance E-REDES's distribution system hosting capacity, the main Portuguese DSO. By sharing its practical experience in implementing market-based flexibility services and non-firm connection agreements, E-REDES seeks to contribute to the broader discussion on grid flexibility and inspire further innovation in the energy sector.

articleTitle: Site selection for battery storage on medium voltage feeders to increase hosting capacity
abstract: In 2022, Hungary announced the installation of at least 33 MW / 66 MWh of battery storage on transmission and distribution systems, to support the integration of variable renewable energy. In the case of the distribution system operators (DSO), the aim of the installations was to increase the hosting capacity of medium voltage (MV) feeders. To maximise the technical potential of the storage units, site selection studies were conducted; present paper details the method and the results of this process using the example of 6 real MV feeders. During the simulations, normal operating conditions were examined, and the symmetry of the network was assumed. To examine the voltage conditions of the lines, we performed time-series, quasi-stationary, one-year power flow calculations. To analyse the voltage regulation possibilities, we also determined the sensitivity factors characteristic of the given network using power flow calculations. In general, the higher the average sensitivity factor of a line, the stronger intervention can be achieved with a given unit of storage capacity. The presented results are suitable for forming a central element of a future strategic plan, which examines the possibility of a roll-out covering the entire service area of DSOs.

articleTitle: Modelling battery storage and flexible connections on LV networks
abstract: The benefits from flexible connections are an untapped resource in LV network planning. Modelling connections such as battery storage systems more accurately would allow network operators to capitalise on the flexibility that these systems offer. This in turn would increase the amount of new demand that can connect to a network and minimise the amount of reinforcement (and therefore cost) required to connect the low carbon technologies needed to meet Net Zero targets. The modelling approach known as Debut or ACE49 is widely used across the UK for designing LV networks. It uses the assumption of normally-distributed demand within a half-hour period to model a realistic worst-case scenario for a network. Debut models were created for a standalone battery, battery-house, and battery-house-PV systems, which represented their expected operating procedures. The methodology allows for bespoke profiles to be created for any size of system using a few key parameters. Model results showed that typical domestic battery storage systems could be expected to reduce peak-hours demand by upwards of 33% per customer, and summer peak exported PV generation by 20%. These profiles would also be immediately available in existing Debut-based network planning tools and accessible to model upwards of 16 million customers.

articleTitle: Experiences from the introduction of a hybrid energy and capacity-based distribution grid tariff in Norway
abstract: The electrification of society increases the strain on the existing electricity infrastructure. Grid tariffs can be used to incentivize lowered customer peak electricity demand and more efficient usage of existing energy infrastructure, thus mitigating costly upgrades of the electricity grid. A public consultation on new tariffs was performed in Norway 2015, and in 2019 the research project ForTa was established with the aim of realizing demand response and reduced investments through an improved introduction of new capacity-based tariffs. On the 1<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">st</sup>of July 2022, a new distribution grid tariff was introduced in Norway. This paper presents some of the analyses and findings from the ForTa project – a point of collaboration between grid operators, industry- and research partners – particularly analyses prior to the introduction of the new tariff, surveys of customer behavior and perception related to the new tariff, and analyses of metered demand data after the introduction of the new tariff. Findings suggest a trend of continued electrification which could lead to increased load peaks and grid challenges but also opportunities for management of such challenges. There are observed redistributional effects of the new tariff, although no clear evidence that the new grid tariff has contributed to household demand response.

articleTitle: Operational load forecasts for dynamic flexibility procurement
abstract: Changes to the management of electricity distribution networks requires the development of essential system operation functions, which include refined forecasting capabilities. The work presented here identifies the most suitable approach to optimise and de-risk the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into demand forecasting functions for operational decision making. As distribution network operators (DNOs) develop their distribution system operation (DSO) functions, a step change is required in their forecasting capability to optimise flexibility procurement. Annual, assumptions-driven models that forecast load at primary and secondary substations will not suffice; operational forecasts at the monthly, weekly and daily level are required to inform flexibility procurement and dispatch decisions that enable deferral of network reinforcement expenditure. This research develops day and week-ahead load forecasting models at primary and secondary substations, utilising the latest advancements in time-series and machine learning methods, to identify flexibility needs and bring procurement of these services closer to the time of use. Development of such capability is critical for network management and has scope for considerable cost efficiencies. Results are presented for the performance of a selection of forecasting methods, partitioned by input data quality and periods of peak demand.

articleTitle: Determination of the maximum LV grid hosting capacity for a rapid integration of photovoltaics, electric vehicles and heat pumps
abstract: With the rapid integration of electric vehicles, heat pumps and photovoltaic systems into the low-voltage grids, the distribution system operators are faced with the challenge of developing their grids. However, traditional grid reinforcements are time and resources consuming and cost-intensive. Therefore, this paper proposes a novel approach based on the monte-carlo simulation to determine the maximum grid hosting capacity. The approach focuses on discovering the weak points in the grids – referred to as bottlenecks – and the critical year when a bottleneck is expected. This is achieved through an iterative monte-carlo distribution of the electric vehicles, heat pumps and photovoltaic systems into the grids in addition to a load flow analysis per distribution. By repeating the calculation for the specific scenario values, the maximum grid hosting capacity is determined per low-voltage grid. To deduce the maximum grid hosting capacity, the bottlenecks and the critical year for all low-voltage grids operated by a distribution system operator, the results of the weak point analysis are fed into a forecast tool. This tool scales the results of the weak point analysis results of selected representative low-voltage grids to all remaining low-voltage grids. Hence, the maximum grid hosting capacity is determined for low-voltage grids.

articleTitle: Distribution system operation considering PV forecasting probability distribution based on sky status
abstract: The intermittent outputs from photovoltaic (PV) based on weather conditions make distribution network management difficult. Probabilistic methods using a probability distribution, such as normal or beta distribution, have been proposed to address this issue. However, an error occurs during the actual power generation, which may pose limitations in expressing it as a single distribution. Accordingly, assuming PV uncertainty as a probability distribution, a prediction error occurs and affects the voltage operation of the distribution network. A voltage control method based on the on-load tap changer was proposed herein that considers the overvoltage generation probability derived via Monte Carlo simulation and a PV generation model according to the sky status. In addition, the effectiveness of the proposed method in hosting capacity analysis compared with that of the method wherein a single distribution is used.

articleTitle: Analysis of distribution system operation effects considering uncertainty in electric vehicle response
abstract: Through the operation of a controllable load, it is possible to contribute to solving voltage problems caused by the output volatility of renewable energy. Having a controllable energy load is one feature of the electric vehicles (EVs). Unlike centrally controlled resources, EV can affect demand response capacity depending on the willingness of EV owners to participate in demand division. Therefore, it is effective for distribution system operators to operate the systems with consideration given to the uncertainty of the willingness response of each EV owner to solve the voltage problem. In this study, we propose a novel method that considers the uncertainty of EV owner response and applies it to solving the renewable energy overvoltage problem. EV charging for each study group was modelled based on the probability distribution by clustering based on the reaction of each EV owner compared to their past response. The probability of overvoltage problem resolution and the EV reaction according to the combination of each study group were analysed.

articleTitle: Capacitive transfer system cables provide inherent voltage support in response to rapidly changing supply and demand
abstract: The transition to a sustainable energy system creates challenges in connecting new demand and generation while ensuring distribution networks operate within regulatory limits. Use of Capacitive Transfer System (CTS) cable constitutes a significant change in power system design, providing benefits through a reduction in line reactance. These include enhanced power delivery, improved power factor and lower voltage drop in comparison with the existing conventional cables. This paper explains the concept of CTS and its benefits relative to existing assets when applied in a case study for a distribution network. When CTS is employed in a network with significant demand and generation connections, CTS reduces the magnitude of a network’s voltage changes in response to intermittent generation and fluctuating demand. CTS improves a network’s hosting capacity within regulatory limits, reducing the need for further costly mitigations.

articleTitle: Methodology for activation of flexible resources and BESSs for optimal voltage support in medium voltage distribution grid
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative approach for the optimal utilization of flexible resources in voltage control, thereby mitigating the need for immediate power system upgrades in distribution grids facing voltage challenges. The proposed methodology focuses on pre-planning the activation of the most cost-effective flexible resources 24 hours in advance, based on load and generation predictions and a market for flexible resources. An Optimal Power Flow (OPF) problem is designed to minimize the overall cost incurred by flexible resources, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESSs) managed by the Distribution System Operator (DSO), and distribution grid losses, all while adhering to voltage and current constraints. The costs associated with the degradation of BESSs due to cycling are accounted for using a nonlinear and adaptable function. Additionally, the paper elucidates a method for real-time updating of the OPF results, triggered by instances such as exceeding voltage or current limits or updates in load predictions. The methodology has been validated across various 24-hour scenarios on a reference grid and has demonstrated a significant reduction in costs for flexible resources incurred by DSOs.

articleTitle: Development of a new SVR for improving PVHC upon voltage drop phenomenon
abstract: Discussions on the installation of photovoltaic (PV) systems in the distribution grid to achieve carbon neutrality are underway. The maximum amount of PV that can be installed is referred to as the PV hosting capacity (PVHC), with one of the limiting factors being voltage deviation. To prevent voltage deviation, voltage regulator devices known as step voltage regulators (SVRs) have been installed in distribution lines. Moreover, the line drop compensation (LDC) method is commonly utilized along with SVRs to estimate and regulate line voltages. In distribution lines with excessive PV integration and long spans, a phenomenon of voltage drop has been observed owing to the significant phase difference between the substation voltage and passing current. The utilization of the LDC method along with SVR cannot effectively manage nonlinear voltage fluctuations, such as voltage drop phenomena, potentially resulting in a decrease in the PVHC owing to voltage estimation errors. Further, the inability to flexibly adjust set values poses a challenge. Therefore, we developed an SVR by utilizing a new voltage estimation formula (new control method). This study focuses on voltage management and assesses whether the PVHC can be enhanced by utilizing the new control method (the new SVR).

articleTitle: Advanced analytics extending network capacity access in operational DERMS
abstract: Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems (DERMS) provide a backbone platform that facilitates integration of various smart grid applications instrumental to the evolution of DER control in distribution systems. This paper explores the operational considerations of three advanced analytics applications: network model-based analytics, operational forecasting, and DER optimisation. Through a lens of experience based on its operational DERMS deployments, Smarter Grid Solutions (SGS) explores seven existing applications of advanced analytics and the considerations required to succeed in an applied, operational context for the modern distribution utility.

articleTitle: Electrifying railway station parking: enhancing Scotland's sustainable mobility
abstract: Recognising the importance of mass electrification of transport demand and the reduction of energy demand, the Scottish Government has committed to reducing car kilometres travelled by 20% by 2030. This necessitates a reduction in the number of daily car journeys and an overall change in attitude towards how cars are used. With an expected increase in the number of commuters using multi-modal travel and low carbon public transport infrastructure there is an increasing need for EV charging infrastructure to support the transition between different travel options. At present, there are 162 EV chargers installed across 17% of Scotland’s rail stations with 64% of rail stations accommodating vehicle parking. This study considers the hypothesis that rail stations located in different geographic areas with different levels of available parking will have unique EV charging infrastructure requirements leading to varying impact on distribution networks. A geospatial analysis of existing EV charging installations is first carried out, followed by a statistical hosting capacity assessment of the network infrastructure located at two rail station sites. The research provides valuable insights for local government, distribution network planners, and stakeholders in the transport sector, facilitating the development of sustainable integrated mobility ecosystems.

articleTitle: Exploiting the solar photovoltaic potential of metropolitan areas with congested networks
abstract: The long-term urban development concept of Budapest, Hungary emphasizes the necessity of increasing renewable energy sources, particularly solar energy, aligning with the Climate Strategy's goal to boost solar photovoltaic capacities from 200 MW to 1, 500 MW by 2030. The city has established a solar cadastre, revealing a maximal technical potential of 5, 000 MW, which is significantly more than the estimated uptake capacity of the already congested electric network. The grid itself is also transforming; ongoing infrastructural developments include residential and office buildings, commercial centres, and land projects, each with varying power requirements, and the rise in new technologies, heat pumps, electric cars, and air conditioners further influences energy demand. Districts IX, XI, XIII are anticipated to experience substantial power growth. However, Budapest's substations face challenges such as a lack of transformation capacity, insufficient medium-voltage feeders, and available land. Thus, the optimal allocation of new photovoltaic capacities within the city is crucial. The study categorizes residential buildings based on structure, geometry, cost, and construction time for solar plant installation. Districts XVIII, XVII, III demonstrate the highest solar potential due to their expansive areas and diverse building structures. Districts I, V, VI exhibit the lowest potential, hindered by regulatory restrictions on installation.

articleTitle: Impact of internal and network-side demand factors in network-serving load management systems
abstract: This contribution presents the impact of internal and network-side demand factors in load management systems according to section 14a of the German Energy Industry Act using the example of charging points for electric vehicles. A methodology to generate network-side demand factors for charging points is presented and applied for average power from 1 kW to 11 kW. Load management is then integrated in a tool for automated strategic network planning. For 2 different real low-voltage networks internal and network-side demand factors are applied in 4 different cases and impact on network state and reinforcement costs is analysed. The simulations show that demand factors have a significant impact on network state. For both low-voltage networks load management only has a positive influence on network state when demand factors are applied. Based on the observations made in this contribution it is recommended to apply network-side demand factors when simulating the impact of load management on low-voltage networks.

articleTitle: Monitoring and control of DER using AMI equipment SMGW and smart meter
abstract: Due to the nature of DER(Distribution Energy Resource), it is difficult to establish a system for separate monitoring and control. As a result, the SMGW and Smart Meter, which are installed to monitor and control DER at the distribution system interconnection point of DER, were added to make it easier to build the system. SMGW was equipped with DNP3.0 and LwM2M protocols for information transfer between ADMS(Advanced Distribution Management System) and AMI systems. Active power control, power factor control, and inverter start and stop are possible through remote commands in the ADMS system, and the performance was verified through field trial application. For voltage control of DER, the volt-bar algorithm was installed and its effectiveness was verified in the actual distribution system. For communication connection with solar inverters, a KSGA spec-based communication protocol was used, and the DPI (Deep Packet Inspection) function was applied to secure security between SMGW and solar inverters. The Smart Meter is capable of monitoring DER through the function of detecting power outages and transmitting push, and the function of storing 50th order harmonics and waveforms.

articleTitle: Coordinated control schemes for improved DER hosting capacity and flexibility provision
abstract: In the future, efficient utilization of all potential flexible energy resources from different voltage levels is needed to fulfill simultaneously the flexibility needs of local distribution system operator (DSO) and system-wide transmission system operator (TSO) in a coordinated way. This paper studies coordinated and frequency level-dependent distributed energy resources’ (DERs’) control and adaptive on-load-tap-changer (OLTC) management scheme to enable prioritized flexibility services provision for the DSOs and TSO. The main idea is that the coordination of flexibilities utilization between distribution and transmission system operators is done depending on the frequency deviation severity. During smaller frequency deviations priority is on DSO needs and during larger frequency deviations priority is on TSO needs in order to support the frequency stability of the whole power system. However, the overall target is to increase DERs’ hosting capacity in the DSO network and increase their availability for the TSO flexibility services provision during the smaller frequency deviations. In this paper, the effect of different DERs’ reactive power control schemes, their location and type of distribution feeders are studied with multiple PSCAD simulations.

articleTitle: Demand-side energy storage configuration discrimination method based on improved correlation analysis
abstract: Due to the intermittency and unpredictability characteristics of renewable energy generation, energy storage can alleviate the difficulties of peak shaving in the power system, increase distribution system hosting capacity, and promote the consumption of renewable energy in the power grid. Under the context of distribution system, this paper introduces a method for identifying optimal user-side energy storage configurations to effectively balance power supply and demand. Firstly, a user-side energy consumption behaviour indicator system is established. Secondly, an improved correlation analysis method that comprehensively considers the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients is proposed to simplify the indicator system and obtain key evaluation indicators. Finally, based on the historical real electricity consumption data of 6670 users in a certain area of Shanghai, the rationality of the method adopted in this paper is verified. Through the study of user-energy storage evaluation technology, providing reference for power grid planning and operational decision-making, thereby effectively evaluating and optimizing the hosting capacity of the distribution system.

articleTitle: Improving LV networks hosting capacity via the use of a neutral point compensator - a Monte-Carlo analysis
abstract: Due to the rapid increase in residential PV capacity, it gets more and more difficult for an LV grid to absorb power at peak hours due to overvoltage issues, causing concerns to DSOs and prosumers who are temporarily unable to inject power into the grid. Monte-Carlo simulations were performed with a parametrized LV feeder model and with input parameters representing typical feeder characteristics in Belgium that could lead to overvoltage occurrences, in order to gain insights on the effectiveness of using a zigzag transformer as neutral point compensator to mitigate the issue. The simulations’ outputs highlighted that such mitigation measure can bring significant voltage excursion (|V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ph-N</sub>- V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">nom</sub>|) reductions. Reductions typically comprised between 14% and 28% have been observed when the zigzag transformer is located near the end of the LV feeder, depending on the zigzag transformer impedance considered. The corresponding reduction of the risk for overvoltage occurrences was comprised between 41% and 77%. The neutral point compensator is only as effective as the unbalance level in the LV feeder, which is linked to the distribution of 1ph PV inverters and 3ph PV inverters on the feeder. The neutral point compensator can thus be regarded as a promising mitigation measure against PV-related overvoltages but with limited effectiveness depending on the unbalance level of the PV production.

articleTitle: ADMS and DERMS utilizing distributed resources for efficient local and system constraint management
abstract: The continuous development of Hong Kong and the ongoing decarbonisation of the energy sector pose challenges to the power grid operated by CLP Power Hong Kong Limited (CLP Power). By efficiently performing constraint management on the local network level and the overall system level, CLP Power can avoid inefficient reinforcements. This constraint management shall be achieved in the future by using the currently being deployed system architecture, including the Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) and the Customer Distributed Energy Resource Management System (C-DERMS). The ADMS will provide key features including the load and constraint identification in the distribution grid. The direct integration with the C-DERMS allows the subsequent location-based and economically optimised activation of customer-owned resources to provide flexibility for resolving the identified network constraints. The resource dispatch can also be performed across the overall supply area to provide flexibility for system constraint management. Future developments can include the enhancement of the dispatch optimisation algorithm of the C-DERMS and the integration of other customer-owned resources and utility-owned battery storages.

articleTitle: Facilitating large-scale integration of RES while maintaining system reliability through the use of flexibility and asset intelligence (ORKEST)

authors.preferredName: P. C. J. M. van der Wielen

abstract: The speed at which renewable energy sources (RES) are entering distribution power networks is unforeseen and disruptive. The need for extra hosting capacity in the distribution grids is huge and cannot always be timely met with network reinforcements. As a result, there is a need to increase the hosting capacity of existing networks. While network operators try to support the energy transition by making as much network capacity available as they can, there are also concerns on the trade-off with asset management aspects like service- and component reliability. At the same time, innovative techniques such as hard- and soft switching, flexibility, temporary overloading of network components and using storage and conversion are not that well embedded in the design toolkit of the network developer and asset manager. In this article, we describe a framework which integrates network capacity and asset/service reliability in an integrated decision framework, enabling lifecycle system aware power network design and -operation.

articleTitle: An analytic probabilistic hosting capacity assessment method for low voltage distribution networks
abstract: There has been an increase in the capacity of distributed energy resources (DERs) integrated into distribution networks, in some cases even surpassing that of utility-scale systems. However, the integration of DERs is complicated by the inherent uncertainties related to their deployment and operations, termed as planning and operational uncertainties. Accurate modeling of these uncertainties is crucial for ensuring the precision of hosting capacity (HC) assessments and optimizing DER integration. State-of-the-art HC methods typically involve stochastic simulation of planning uncertainties through a Monte-Carlo simulation (MCS) and propagation of operational uncertainties using a probabilistic load flow method (PLF). This involves multi-tier iterations of the load flow, assessing the impacts of a range of input scenarios, including random DER placement, DER power variability, and penetration range. While the multi-scenario approach in the stochastic HC (SHC) methods enhances HC accuracy, they are computationally intensive, limiting their scalability and practical applicability. This study proposes a streamlined approach that replaces the stochastic simulation of planning uncertainties with an analytic approach. In this approach, planning uncertainty is characterized using a probability density function (PDF) and combined, as a product, with the PDF model of the operational uncertainties. The unified probabilistic function is thus used to represent the combined uncertainty, enabling a single-pass computation of the HC through an analytic PLF method. The proposed analytic HC (AHC) method is tested on a sample residential LV feeder, with a loading typical of suburban areas in South Africa. The resulting performance is compared to that of a state-of-the-art SHC method. The proposed AHC method records significant improvement in computational efficiency (>1000x) while maintaining comparable performance to the SHC method. This development enables fast, reliable, and scalable DER integration assessments by distribution network operators.

articleTitle: Analysing the interaction of expansion decisions by end customers and grid development in the context of a municipal energy system
abstract: In order to achieve greenhouse gas neutrality by 2045, the Climate Protection Act sets emission reduction targets for the years 2030 and 2040, as well as decreasing annual emission volumes for some sectors, including the building sector. Measures to decarbonize the building sector include energy retrofits and the expansion of renewable, decentralized power generators and low-CO2 heat generators. These measures thus change both the load and the generation of the future energy supply concept. Considering the interactions of the changed installed technologies on the building level and their influence on the electrical grid infrastructure is necessary. The grid operator will remedy the future congested grid states by grid expansion measures and pass on the costs to the connected grid users, which in turn could influence their behaviour and decisions. The aim of this work is a holistic analysis of the staggered interactions of generation expansion and grid expansion for a future decentralized energy supply concept conditioned by the expansion in the field of self-generation. To enable the analysis of the interactions, a multi-criteria optimization procedure for expansion and operation decisions at the building level is combined with an approach to determine grid expansion. As part of this work, the effect of an expansion of hosting capacity on the grid charges and thus the decision-making behaviour was investigated.

articleTitle: Empowering consumers through smart meter technology
abstract: Elenia, Finland's second largest distribution network operator, launched an innovative initiative called AinaLab. As a distribution network operator, Elenia operates mainly in rural areas, with 175 metres of network per customer. This experimental service utilizes next-generation smart meter technology to provide real-time measurement and insights into electricity consumption. Available free of charge to customers, AinaLab empower users to understand and optimize their energy usage. By focusing on agility and experimentation, customers are provided straightforward solutions without excessive fine-tuning times, and successful results are integrated into the customer's extranet, Elenia Aina. Users get detailed information about their home's electricity system, allowing them to make informed decisions to save energy and reduce their carbon footprint. Based on feedback from customers, the service is easy and straightforward to use. The broader objective is to improve the daily lives of customers while driving innovation in the energy sector, awaiting national demand response models.

articleTitle: DSSE as a tool for hosting capacity assessment in European-type distribution grids
abstract: The use of distribution system state estimation (DSSE) can enhance the hosting capacity of an electrical distribution system (DS). DSSE allows for an accurate assessment of the DS state, to integrate a higher share of distributed energy resources. However, due to the low rate of the advanced metering infrastructure deployment in several European countries, some customers still not equipped with smart meters. In turn this limits the implementation of DSSE in the DS. Furthermore, most of distribution system operators consider the constant power load model in carrying out the power flow analysis. This leads to get biased results because of relying on an inaccurate load model. In this context, the paper proposes an efficient DSSE approach to overcome the problems addressed above. This is done by considering modelling the load as a ZIP model using the load profiles recovered by a top-down load forecasting method based on the feeder measurements and the customer information system. The ZIP model is incorporated as an equality constraint in the augmented Lagrangian based DSSE, while the recovered load profile is utilized as the nominal power at the rated voltage. A numerical analysis is conducted to highlight the significant improvement provided by the proposed approach.

articleTitle: Development of wireless vehicle-to-grid (V2G) for flexible resource utilization of autonomous vehicles
abstract: In the current global scenario where the adoption of electric vehicles is rapidly increasing, if electric cars can efficiently utilize surplus power, they can play a role as a new flexible resource in microgrid distributed energy systems. This would maximize the efficiency of distributed energy systems, further activating the distribution of renewable energy. Additionally, the development of mobility with large-capacity batteries, such as electric shuttles with autonomous driving technology, is expected to function as mobile flexible resources, moving without the need for a driver. Furthermore, creation of value flows between autonomous vehicle owners, charging service providers, and grid operators could be enabled, allowing for consideration of business expansion in the power sector. Building a platform that seamlessly integrates Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) systems and power systems through Virtual Power Plants (VPP) and utilizing autonomous vehicle driving-related data for power market predictions are expected to create revenue models. To illustrate this, we introduce the upcoming demonstration project on wireless charging V2G-based autonomous shuttles in Korea's Energy Valley.

articleTitle: Implementation of distribution network development plans according to EU directive 2019/944: possibilities for automation
abstract: To support the integration of renewable energy sources, and increase the transparency for flexibility requirements, EU released the EU directive 2019/944. It enforces distribution system operators to develop network development plans (NDPs) for their respective networks. This paper present the results from an interview study conducted to gain insights from some of the member states that have already implemented the directive, to learn from their experience. The study found overall that current systems inability to export and share data through simple means requires large amount of resources from the DSOs. Furthermore the role of flexibility in NDPs was analysed. With more flexibility from the demand side it was found that behaviour scenario will play a vital role in order to assess the hosting capacity.

articleTitle: Technical solutions enabling network operation with high share of DER and dynamic loads in CEZ Distribuce (DSO)
abstract: The paper describes technical solutions and approaches supporting secure operation of distribution networks with distributed energy resources (DER) and dynamic loads. The solutions are implemented as business as usual by CEZ Distribuce, the largest DSO in the Czech Republic (with approx. 3.8 million supply points). The aim is to meet the growing number of customer requirements (especially in terms of DER connected to the distribution network) related to EU policy and National Action Plan for Smart Grids in the Czech Republic and still being able to operate distribution network safely with required power quality. The paper also discusses other measures for possible future network operation such as energy storage, non-firm connections, flexibility provision etc.

articleTitle: Electrifing heat: innovations in network capacity management for medium voltage sites
abstract: Electrification is expected to play a major role in heat decarbonisation. This is expected to place significant additional burdens upon electricity distribution networks, especially for winter peaking networks. This paper examines an innovative approach to the managing decarbonisation of heat through electrification to large complex sites, connected to the Medium Voltage network, by providing options to site developers to help them minimise the cost of any necessary network upgrades.

articleTitle: The impact of increased information content on electricity load forecasting
abstract: Electricity load forecasting of private households usually aims at predicting the household’s total load by applying artificial intelligence methods to data measured at the household’s grid connection point. This is a challenging task, as the parameter of interest is influenced by climate, seasonal and human factors. With the rising number of implemented digital metering systems, future household data promises to not only contain the total load, but also to have an increased granularity, even covering the load of single household devices. This analysis investigates the extent to which the knowledge of the per-device load will improve the residential load forecasting quality by training an artificial neural network (ANN) on the data taken at the grid connection point and comparing its results to the collective output of ANNs trained on high-granularity data containing every individual electricity load in the household.

articleTitle: Improving LV networks hosting capacity via the use of residential P-Q inverter control – a Monte-Carlo analysis
abstract: Due to the rapid increase in residential PV capacity, it gets more and more difficult for an LV grid to absorb power at peak hours due to overvoltage issues, causing concerns to DSOs and prosumers who are temporarily unable to inject power into the grid. In collaboration with Belgian DSOs and via the use of metered consumption and injection data, dedicated Monte-Carlo analyses were performed to investigate mitigation measures. The focus in this paper is the use of P-Q control strategies of residential PV inverters, which could allow to significantly reduce the overvoltage occurrences and severity. Even though only some countries already have a clearly defined regulatory framework for such use of residential PV inverters, it is worthy to analyze the potential benefits of this approach. Losses of energy production were first assessed for each control method. A parametrized LV feeder was modelled in Digsilent Powerfactory and Monte-Carlo simulations were performed, with variations of different input parameters and randomly assigned consumer/prosumer load and injection profiles based on an existing set of households’ data, as well as different strategies of P-Q inverter control. Thanks to thousands of simulations, the risk for overvoltage occurrences was assessed (focusing on periods with max irradiance). Besides the impact of different parameters such as the feeder’s length or the amount of houses with PV on the feeder, a specific attention was paid to the beneficial impact of using the different P-Q control strategies. Dedicated KPI’s regarding the impact on prosumer households were analyzed and the best P-Q control strategies were discussed.

articleTitle: Phase balancing to increase LV network headroom: phase switch system trial
abstract: The proliferation of Electric Vehicle (EV) charging, Heat Pumps (HP), and Photo Voltaic (PV) generation within low voltage (LV) distribution networks is expected to escalate. This growth will cause congestion, triggering reinforcement needs to increase hosting capacity (HC) and maintain power quality and continuity. This paper presents findings from a Phase Switch System (PSS) deployment trial on the UK Power Networks (UKPN) distribution network in London and Brighton. The patented PSS increases HC by dynamically balancing three-phase LV distribution mains (LV-main) through real-time phase switching of conductors. With 2023 loads, results from the trial LV-main that supplies 40 customers, increased HC by up to 232A and 202A on average. Also, it provided an estimated 28 MWh annual energy savings in losses reductions. Crucially, simulations of future 7kW electric vehicle charging loads indicate that over 5 years, the PSS could provide 31A per phase more HC than a new and additional cable rated 500A per phase. This comparison to new cables is made, as the HC they provide is widely understood. The trial showcased the PSS as a flexible, rapidly deployable, cost-effective solution to reduce losses and unlock HC, for low-carbon technology integration into LV networks.

articleTitle: Automation approach of RES hosting capacity estimation in the distribution network using PowerFactory software
abstract: This article presents the RES hosting capacity estimation Module which allow calculate maximum RES generation for each node of the distribution network, considering different simulation scenarios and requirements of the ‘(N-1) reliability criterion’ in DIgSILENT PowerFactory software. The Module solves two main tasks. The first task covers the calculation of the allowable RES value for selected terminals (nodes) of the network. The second task is concerned with the calculation of the maximum RES generation in the middle of each line (due to the possible connection of RES to the existing lines). The module can solve both tasks very quickly, simultaneously, or separately, depending on the users’ settings. Finally, the Module generates output files and tables with the detailed calculation results. This approach was realised using Python programming language. The Module has been already employed in power system operator. The proposed approach, software and calculation results can be used to perform a cost-benefit analysis at the stage of the feasibility study of the renewable power plant construction by potential investors. This information will be important both for existing and for perspective development plans of the power system.

articleTitle: Regulatory experimentation as a tool to test innovative solutions to enhance flexibility markets deployment in Europe
abstract: Regulatory experimentation is recognised as a key tool by different sector stakeholders and regulatory authorities to test innovative products and services that are not yet permitted within current regulatory frameworks. In the energy sector, regulatory experiments are used to test solutions in different areas such as flexibility, which is a crucial topic for the energy transition since it allows electricity grid operators to manage situations with an increased peak demand and contributes to the grid stability and reliability. This paper explores the existing flexibility related regulatory frameworks and experiments at the European level, focusing on how their results can allow the deployment of flexibility markets in Europe, and the improvement and harmonisation of the European regulatory framework.

articleTitle: A large-scale study of the impact of future unregulated EV charging on low voltage grids
abstract: The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption prompts crucial questions regarding the resilience and capacity of low voltage (LV) grids to meet the escalating demands of widespread EV charging. This study investigates the dynamic landscape of EV charging and its implications on LV networks in a federal state in Austria, shedding light on the resilience and capacity of the networks. In examining two EV charging use cases: private EV charging with car sharing, and fleet charging, the study delves into the specific dynamics of each use case. Additionally, the integration of photovoltaic (PV) systems and heat pumps (HPs), which will constitute a substantial proportion of electricity generation and consumption respectively in the future are examined. While quasi-dynamic load flow calculations show severe network violations in voltage and line/transformer loading in over 75% of the LV networks by the year 2040, the problems are exacerbated in worst-case load flow calculations. The seamless integration of PV is hindered by the mismatch between EV charging times and PV generation periods.

articleTitle: Dynamic line rating in HV distribution grid – experiences and initial hosting capacity analysis
abstract: In this paper we present an ongoing project in which the high voltage distribution grid of Elvia, a Norwegian DSO, with 3200 km of lines, will be monitored using overhead line sensors (Heimdall Power’s Neurons) and advanced software (Heimdall Cloud). Result from the first two months of monitoring of a transmission corridor show that there is significant spare capacity in the line most of the time, but that DLR purely based on weather forecasts, overestimates the capacity a large part of the time, compared to the sensor-based DLR. A method to visualise hosting capacity based on DLR is presented, and preliminary results show that in order to really exploit the benefits of DLR for hosting capacity increase at the distribution level, active grid management must evolve to allow for situations where the expected base-line load can become higher than the capacity for a certain percentage of the time.

articleTitle: Enhancing DER interconnection through hosting capacity with mitigation solutions
abstract: Hosting capacity analytics have traditionally been used to identify the amount of generation or load that can be accommodated on the grid without requiring upgrades. These analytics support utilities in their interconnection processes but fail to identify solutions to integrate load or generation when upgrades are required. Advances in hosting capacity analytics have enabled the study to go beyond simple accommodation and now consider mitigation solutions. The objective of this paper is to present this advanced hosting capacity method to enable integration of resources.

articleTitle: Improving LV networks hosting capacity via the use of voltage stabilizers – lab testing and simulation models for de-risking field deployment
abstract: Due to the rapid increase in residential PV capacity, it gets more and more difficult for an LV grid to absorb power at peak hours due to overvoltage issues, causing concerns to DSOs and prosumers who are temporarily unable to inject power into the grid. Short-term solutions to control voltage in low voltage feeders were investigated, with the goal to ensure that all installed PV capacity can flow in a secure, reliable and uninterrupted manner in the low voltage distribution grid. Working in collaboration with Belgian DSOs, two voltage regulators were tested to their limits in a controlled lab environment before deployment onsite in the scope of pilot projects of Belgian DSOs, to provide insights and guidelines to DSOs for de-risking the future field deployment of such devices. The voltage stabilizer (or Line Voltage Regulator – LVR) can inject voltages in both down and up directions to either reduce and increase the voltage at its output, compared to its input. Lab testing gave a better understanding of the technology’s limits, helped the different parties make the best technological choices based on facts and numbers, and limited any risks associated with the roll-out of this innovative solution. Based on the lab results, a simulation model of the LVR was developed for further de-risking the roll-out of the devices by considering multiple installation use cases.

articleTitle: Utilizing electricity price signals for load control using smart meter
abstract: During the 2022 energy crisis, fixed-rate electricity prices surged, prompting a preference for spot electricity contracts. Consumers using spot electricity sought to shift consumption to cheaper hours. Traditionally many owners of electrically heated buildings in Finland have moved electricity heating to night hours (22-07) through electricity meters control signals, resulting in more affordable electricity prices. These users have requested DSOs to adjust controls to even later times, given the frequent high prices of electricity in the late evening hours. Elenia realized an opportunity to support the consumers to transfer the consumption automatically to lower-priced hours. A load control service allowing customers to utilize the two load control relays attached to the smart meters was developed. The relays can be connected own devices such as a water heater or EV charger. The customers have an option to define their preferred hours for the relays or choose to have the relays follow the lowest spot price including the DSO’s lower night tariffs. The service handles daily meter reconfigurations after the next day's spot prices are published. This is the first service directly leveraging smart meters for customers and building upon it an intelligent service and bringing added value to customers.

articleTitle: Comparative techno-economic analysis of distribution network reinforcement and LEC flexibility for overvoltage regulation
abstract: This paper aims to investigate the economic viability of line upgrades, battery energy storage systems (BESS), optimized active photovoltaic (PV) power curtailment, and the utilization of reactive power from PV inverters to handle overvoltage problems in distribution grids. To do this, we propose a line upgrade investment model to pinpoint lines requiring reinforcement. An optimization model is developed for BESS to optimize charge/discharge schedules for demand and generation balancing. To minimize the need for active PV power curtailment, an optimization based curtailment strategy is also proposed, which ensures grid voltage constraints are met. Simulations on a real-world distribution grid highlight the increasing costs of line upgrades with higher PV penetration. While simulations indicate BESS can technically address overvoltage issues, they may not be the most cost-effective approach, particularly compared to active PV curtailment and reactive power injection from PV inverters.

articleTitle: Impact of fast frequency response on renewable energy source curtailment and load shedding
abstract: System operators in low-inertia power systems often have to curtail renewable energy sources (RES) and employ strict under-frequency load shedding (UFLS) schemes to ensure frequency security after an event leading to loss of generation. This approach limits the maximum RES penetration in a system and results to the loss of load. To tackle these problems, fast frequency response (FFR) schemes can be used to limit the frequency Nadir after a disturbance and decrease the need for RES curtailments and UFLS. This article provides insights on the interaction between the Kinetic Energy (KE), Frequency Containment Reserves (FCR), and Nadir after a disturbance, which are the driving mechanisms leading to RES curtailment. Then, it analyses the impact of FFR on the Nadir and its ability to alleviate RES curtailment problems. The low-inertia, islanded, Cyprus dynamic model is used to quantify the results and showcase the impact on a real system.

articleTitle: A review of energy management strategies with a focus on hosting capacity in modern energy systems
abstract: Renewable energy sources (RES) power output is variable and intermittent consisting of predictable and unpredictable fluctuations. Large-scale integration of RES requires solutions like energy storages to manage the increased intermittency. Management of energy flow among various generation and storage systems becomes crucial when multiple sources are integrated to the power system. To optimize power system performance and minimize negative impacts of RES, sizing of the storage components and energy management strategies and solutions become essential. The energy management, often using some optimization techniques, aims to ensure reliable and cost-efficient electricity supply and distribution. The details of energy management strategy depend on the type of network, its components and connected controllable energy resources. This review focuses on energy management strategies with a primary interest on hosting capacity (HC). Widespread adoption of distributed generation (DG) in distribution networks has increased different challenges and violations of operational limits. These issues include overvoltage, undervoltage, excessive line losses, transformer and feeder overloads, protection failures, and elevated harmonic distortion levels. Such problems arise when the distribution network exceeds its HC limit. This review includes an examination of HC’s evolution, methodologies, and implications for grid resilience and sustainability.

articleTitle: Feasibility study of a renewable energy community development using hydrogen
abstract: The analysis of energy communities is an important area of current power system research. In this feasibility study, energy data was gathered for an industrial site with an annual electricity consumption of around 300 MWh, plus an additional 300 MWh for transportation. A time-series energy model was proposed for analysis, encompassing solar energy production, electricity usage, hydrogen production via electrolysis, storage, and its application in transportation. Specific system components and cost-benefit analyses for a potential pilot site were examined. The model allowed for up to 600 kW<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">p</sub>of solar photovoltaic capacity, with estimations of energy potentials and constraints including electrolyser power limits, compression energy demands, storage technicalities, and operational profiles. The study's key contribution lies in establishing a time series model applicable not only to the studied site but also to similar energy communities. It enables scenario analysis for different configurations at various time scales, accounting for system losses. Results indicate the potential for three vehicle charges of 8 kg hydrogen per day, with annual hydrogen generation ranging from 776 kg to 8000 kg and storage capacity from 20m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>to 180 m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>. The study suggests potential cooperation between renewable energy communities, green mobility, and the distribution system, offering insights into mitigating local network congestions, and through that increasing the hosting capacity of power systems.

articleTitle: Distributed optimization in energy communities: a focus on flexibility provision
abstract: The emergence of energy communities (ECs) as new stakeholders in modern electrical grids presents an opportunity to address the challenges associated with integrating distributed energy resources, such as increased uncertainty and variability in generation, transmission grid saturation, or diminished power quality, among others. The ability of an EC to provide flexibility is therefore paramount. However, data privacy and investment costs are the main drawbacks to achieving optimal operation. This paper proposes a distributed optimization framework designed for the economic dispatch (ED) of ECs, employing the auxiliary problem principle (APP) decomposition technique. The primary focus is to study the effects of flexibility provision in real-time control while addressing data privacy concerns and minimizing communication infrastructure investments. The proposed algorithm is tested in a case study, providing insights into the selection of the control parameters of the APP framework to improve the convergence properties.

articleTitle: Innovative power line management solutions based on dynamic line rating technology
abstract: As both electricity generation and consumption trends change rapidly nowadays, Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) technology is becoming more and more popular in case of transmission and distribution grids. Depending on the goal of its application, it is an efficient way of handling controlled temporary or long-term overloads, increase operational safety, provide solutions for anti-icing, or even gather a large number of input data for asset management expert systems by sensors installed in the grid. However, a gap has been identified between the manufacturing side and the end-users, especially regarding the determination of the number and the position of required devices on-site. GridGuard, as a product of the DLR research group of Budapest University of Technology and Economics, offers completely novel solutions in the framework of its own Dynamic Line Rating expert system like critical span analysis, taking cooling effects of precipitation into account, or using AI-based calculations to introduce the “sensor rental” philosophy on the market. In this paper, based on our concept, the so-called distributed sensor allocation method is introduced together with our virtual sensor philosophy replacing on-site devices after the learning period. The key of our sensor number and position identification is the “know more, achieve more” philosophy. As expected reliability is specified by the user, the required number of monitored tension spans and sensor positions are determined. To achieve high accuracy, sometimes a relatively large number of devices is required. Based on our principles of DLR, this can be achieved cost-effectively with our simplified sensors measuring only the necessary physical quantities from the aspect of our calculating algorithms, based on the extension of well-known international models. Novel GridGuard DLR concept offers both real-time and predicted ampacity (DLR), anti-icing features, together with own sensor device and weather station. In this paper, we would like to highlight how our expert system is unique, offering essential data for the operators to enhance the utilization of their grid, and to help providing safe and clean energy as the base of tomorrow’s power market.

articleTitle: Restructuring of distribution systems through clustering of voltage sensitivity to PV presence
abstract: Distributed photovoltaic micro and mini-generators play a prominent role as they become increasingly accessible to end consumers. They promise to reduce expenses related to electrical energy and potential ﬁnancial returns. One way to improve the application and planning of the distribution network and its hosting capacity is partitioning these systems, using the impact of distributed generation as a criterion. Therefore, this work aims to construct a generic network partitioning method using the Spectral Clustering algorithm adapted with a balancing algorithm to guarantee a certain similarity in the output cluster size. The input data for this method are obtained from modeling actual standardized electrical systems and the simulation of photovoltaic generation individual impact on each low-voltage feeder connected to the primary grid. The voltage sensitivity coefﬁcient is a metric that quantiﬁes the voltage change at one node with the variation of active power at another one. Considering all simulation states, the ratios of these coefﬁcients per node are the Sensitivity matrix elements. By applying Balanced Spectral Clustering to this Sensitivity matrix, the method can provide continuous electrical regions that highlight the optimal partitioning of the tested distribution system. This proposed method may serve as an initial framework to deﬁne, for example, the hosting capacity of smaller regions, considering the characteristics of the electrical system as a whole but managing its restrictive factors locally.

articleTitle: Multiport converter design and optimal location in distribution grids
abstract: Multiport converters (MPC) are presented as a general power electronics solution that can contribute to facilitate a massive integration of distributed renewable generation while enhancing the interconnection of multiple electrical grids and equipment. The MPC implement an integrated solution combining the advantages of energy storage and other grid support equipment. This paper presents an optimisation-based methodology to size and allocate multiport power converters together with a techno-economic comparison to other conventional approaches. This methodology includes AC power flow constraints and is evaluated in a case study based on IEEE 33 bus system to identify the best scenarios where multiport converters can be considered as a potential solution.

articleTitle: Unbalance and voltage maintenance control with BESS: laboratory investigations for low-voltage grids
abstract: Laboratory tests investigate controls using one to three single-phase inverters of battery energy storage systems (BESSs) for unbalance reduction and voltage maintenance to keep VUF, k<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">U0</sub>and voltage within the limits of DIN EN 50160. The laboratory setup includes a grid simulator, line impedance, BESS units, unbalanced loads, and measuring systems. The control mechanisms were tested with varied scenarios and loads.
