The control decouples active and reactive power to influence voltage amplitude and phase angle separately. This controls can operate at any grid connection point independently. The system proved fundamentally stable, reducing unbalance and maintaining voltage, though exceptions occurred with low BESS power. Scenarios include varied unbalance loads, grid voltage and varied power and connection of one to three single-phase BESS. Best results involved all three BESSs or matching BESS phase conductors with unbalanced loads. In one case, three active BESSs reduced VUF from 2.55% to 1.49%. The tests provided technical insights into BESS design, implementation, and potential for dynamic unbalance reduction and voltage maintenance in low-voltage grids.

articleTitle: The role of demand-side flexibility in harmonics-considered dynamic hosting capacity
abstract: In this paper, we analyse the potential of demand-side flexibility and the importance of considering higher-order harmonics in calculating distributed energy resources (DERs) hosting capacity in low voltage (LV) distribution networks. We step aside from traditional calculations, in which hosting capacity (HC) is assessed based on the worst-case scenario and calculate dynamic export and import limits, based on near real-time electricity consumption estimates. In the scenario without modelling higher-order harmonics, the results show that upward flexibility contributes to the increase of installed distributed generators since aggregated active power increases between 0.05 and 38%, depending on the case study. When import limits are calculated, dynamic HC (DHC) also increases due to the demand-side flexibility potential, with the impact even more significant than in the case of export. Introducing higher-order harmonics in the model leads to decreased DHC in the scenario in which export limits are calculated. The decrease happens not only because of the total harmonic distortion (THD) constraint but also due to the contribution of the higher-order harmonics to the root-mean-square (RMS) voltage value. When calculating dynamic import limits, harmonic voltages increase the RMS voltage magnitude and, that way, free up additional space for the DERs installation.

articleTitle: Stability of future low-inertia power systems with different grid-forming control schemes
abstract: Different grid-forming and grid-following inverter control and synchronization schemes can affect and support the low-inertia power system frequency stability in different ways. It is of key importance, however, that frequency stability can be always secured with varying shares of grid-forming and grid-following inverters as well as rotating generators. This paper presents case studies with variable shares of two different type of grid-forming inverter-based resources, grid-following inverters and synchronous generators. Case studies are done with a simple power system modelled with PSCAD to study the effect of these resources on frequency stability after a load increase. In overall, paper presents multiple proposals to further improve frequency stability by enhanced control of the studied grid-forming inverters in the simulated cases.

articleTitle: DSO risk management strategies for reducing risk caused by actions in future flexibility markets
abstract: The lack of visibility of the actions of new actors such as aggregators and customers providing demand side response and other ancillary services will present new risks to Distribution System Operators (DSO’s) in both their planning of new investments and in the day to day running of the system. The key question is how will DSO’s identify these potential risks, value them and then act on them to safe guard the operation of their network systems and protect their financial performance? This paper presents a methodology / approach for assessing/quantifying such risks, to help understand the impact of various mitigation strategies. At the heart of this framework, lies an Agent Based Modelling tool, which models the interactions of key agents such as aggregators, generators, independent system/market place operators and domestic/industrial customers.

articleTitle: Optimal distribution system planning integrating soft open points under distributed generation uncertainty
abstract: As load growth and Distributed Generation (DG) connection in distribution systems increase in recent years, network reinforcements are required to avoid security constraint violations. In this context, Sot Open Points (SOPs) appear as a solution to defer network reinforcements by providing active and reactive power regulation. This work proposes a two-stage distribution system planning to cope with load growth and with DG connection under high uncertainty, comparing network reinforcement with SOPs installation. The first stage employs a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) optimization to find the optimal network upgrades (Reinforcement or SOP) based on the expected load growth. The second stage uses a Monte Carlo simulation combined with a Linear Programming DG curtailment minimization to compute expected curtailment for multiple connection scenarios and hosting capacity levels. The results indicate that installing SOP can be advantageous from both economic and DG curtailment point-of-view in comparison to network reinforcements for the case studies considered regardless of hosting capacity target level.

articleTitle: 20 years of hosting capacity studies, 2004 - 2024
abstract: The term “hosting capacity”, as it is used at this conference, was first introduced in March 2004, and has since resulted in a range of applications and research. The concept is commonly used by network operators to quantify the ability of their networks to accept new production and consumption. Academic research on hosting capacity took off seriously after 2010 and has resulted in thousands of publications. This paper presents a brief history of the early years of hosting-capacity studies, gives an overview of the status of both applications and research, and gives some thoughts about the future.

articleTitle: CAPTEN: a service providing access to a map of hosting capacities and a simplified multiple load insertion simulator
abstract: To address the challenges raised by an increasingly decentralized electricity production and the integration of emerging technologies such as EV charging, French DSO Enedis developed the CAPTEN methodology. This approach streamlines the estimation of network hosting capacities in electricity distribution networks by using a fast and simplified load flow method along with linear approximations, reducing calculation time while maintaining accuracy. CAPTEN provides local authorities with a map of hosting capacities, facilitating the identification of optimal locations for plugging new loads. Furthermore, it features a multiple load integration simulator, allowing users to integrate new loads into the network with the hosting capacities map updating accordingly. Building upon CAPTEN's foundation, this paper introduces CEDRE, an innovative tool designed to enhance impact studies for network planning at Enedis. CEDRE efficiently simulates the massive integration of new electrical applications into low voltage networks, swiftly identifying and assessing network constraints. This advancement enables rapid estimation of necessary network reinforcements and associated costs, offering a pragmatic solution for comprehensive network planning amidst evolving electric utilization patterns.

articleTitle: High performance controlled switching vacuum circuit breaker enables fast reclosing on capacitor bank - breakthrough in reactive power compensation
abstract: Today the decentralized power generation (wind farms and photovoltaic plants) is growing more and more. Medium voltage capacitor banks are crucial to assure network stability, reliability, and reactive power compensation. The recent releases of high-performance synchronized vacuum circuit breakers for capacitor switching applications overcome technical challenges like inrush currents, prestrikes and restrikes. These features allow to extend the lifetime of the whole asset, manage the network reducing the need of components for mitigating transients and synergies with other technologies for managing loads transitions (e.g. Static VAR Compensator). This publication presents a breakthrough step of the circuit breaker functionality combining the transient-free and restrike-free functionality with a new fast-reclosing function eliminating the need of discharging time before re-energizing the capacitor bank. A medium voltage (MV) circuit breaker, with its embedded digital control and precise actuation system, is presented together with its capability to combine restrike-free open operation with transient-free close operation at any time, by adapting continuously the closing strategy based on measurements taken on the network and on the load. In this article, the circuit breaker concept and features are presented together with the performances of closing and opening operations performed at any status of charge of capacitor banks, in both simulations and laboratory tests.

articleTitle: Modeling and application of a load management system for controllable appliances for low-voltage network planning
abstract: This contribution investigates the impact of load management system, based on the concretisation of section 14a German Energy Industry Act on the network status of the future supply task. For this purpose, both implementation variants of direct control and energy management system, as well as the prioritised control of individual controllable appliances types are examined. In addition, the influence of internal and network-side demand factors on the network status and the planning results is analysed. Furthermore, an end-year based planning without limited application of a load management system is compared with a two-year based planning with limited application. The contribution demonstrates that the application of internal demand factors and network-side demand factors as well as the prioritisation of controllable appliances have a significant impact on the resulting limit violations. In addition, network operator can reduce network expansion costs by redesigning networks directly for a longer planning horizon instead of only reacting to the reduction of loads with network expansion. In contrast, the application of a load management system according to the current legal situation does not lead to a reduction in costs and should not be considered in target network planning.

articleTitle: Static load modeling during large frequency fluctuations: an experimental investigation with individual devices
abstract: In the past, frequency dependency has often been neglected in load modeling. However, the volatility of frequency is likely to increase in future grid scenarios. To assess novel strategies to increase flexibility in distribution grids, it becomes crucial to accurately model the power response of connected loads to larger frequency fluctuations. The experimental study presented in this paper aims to provide insights into the load behavior of modern load devices in the range 50±6 Hz. The three devices under test represent commonly used load technologies in low-voltage grids. For active and reactive power of each device, we identify three static load models based on steady-state measurements; a lookup table model as a result of interpolation, as well as an exponential model and a linear model based on curve fitting. Then, we assess whether these models can reconstruct the behavior of the devices during dynamic frequency variations. When comparing the measured and reconstructed power, we find the largest deviations for the motor-based load under test. For the power electronic-interfaced load under test, we observe that reactive power is significantly more frequency-dependent than active power. The outcomes of our study can be helpful for novel demand-side management strategies such as frequency-based power control.

articleTitle: Enhancing low voltage network capacity through phase load balance optimization using advanced smart meter data analytics and static reconnections
abstract: This paper addresses the challenges facing low voltage networks amidst global demands for decarbonisation and the integration of dispersed renewable energy sources. As traditional cable upgrades are costly and time-consuming they should be considered as a last resort. We propose a phase load balancing methodology as a cost-effective alternative possible in some scenarios. This approach redistributes loads across different phases to balance phase utilisation, thereby unlocking spare capacity, reducing peak loading, and delaying the need for cable reinforcements. Focusing on low-voltage networks, our methodology evaluates imbalances in conductor sections, identifying systematic imbalance patterns and devising a consumer reconnection plan to mitigate these imbalances. The methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated on an actual network involving a secondary transformer station, with 192 low-voltage conductor sections, and 226 consumers, all equipped with smart meters. We show that most load imbalances are systematic and can be mitigated through static reconnections, increasing capacity by up to 20% in individual sections. Due to low cost, phase load balancing is a great primary response to some capacity constraint scenarios in low-voltage networks.

articleTitle: Operation and control challenges of BESS within distribution networks
abstract: The value proposition of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), based upon participation in the frequency-response market, capacity management and local balancing, has driven a very high penetration level in distribution networks across Great Britain (GB). This paper outlines some identified operation and control challenges of BESS within distribution networks. It explores and reviews different possible solutions to address those challenges and unlock additional hosting capacity, in order allow future Low Carbon Technology (LCT) growth and develop networks fit for the transition to Net Zero.

articleTitle: Impact of local flexibility markets on distribution network hosting capacity
abstract: The paper investigates the influence of local flexibility markets, modelled with autonomous agents, on the hosting capacity of distribution networks. As distributed energy resources (DERs) continue to increase, optimising their integration into distribution grids is crucial for ensuring reliability and resilience. The study is intended to assess how local flexibility markets can positively impact distribution network hosting capacity. The behaviour of diverse market participants, including DERs and flexible loads, is modelled with the agent-based approach. The objective is to quantify the impact of local market dynamics on the hosting capacity of distribution networks. The study explores market structures, pricing mechanisms, and agent strategies to determine the conditions under which significant improvements in hosting capacity can be achieved. The focus is modelling market liquidity and its role in influencing hosting capacity. Realistically simulating market conditions, the research aims to provide quantitative insights into the correlation between local market characteristics and distribution network performance. The outcomes are anticipated to offer valuable information for understanding the potential of local flexibility markets in enhancing hosting capacity.

articleTitle: Active medium-voltage grid coupling using particle swarm optimization
abstract: Distribution grids have constantly evolved to collector grids to meet the goals of the energy transition. For further integration of renewable energy sources (RES), especially wind and solar parks, the technology of a medium-voltage direct current (MVDC) system can increase the hosting capacity and flexibility in the medium-voltage grid level by horizontal active power flow control as well as voltage control on both sides of the system. This paper examines the potential of a MVDC back-to-back converter for power flow reduction with the higher grid level. The methodology focuses on the formulation of the optimization problem and uses the Particle Swarm Optimization to determine the operating points of the MVDC system, while load and generation profiles as well as grid constraints and asset limits are considered. For the case study, real grid topology and asset data as well as load and generation in an existing distribution grid is used to estimate the reduction of power exchange between the medium-voltage (MV) and the high-voltage (HV) grid level. The results show the potential of different sizes of the MVDC system. In the best scenario, the HV/MV power exchange can be reduced by 24% over the period of one week with high RES in-feed.

articleTitle: Detection of electric vehicle charging events in low voltage networks: enhancing load visibility for network planning
abstract: Integrating electric vehicles (EVs) into low voltage (LV) networks introduces non-linear loads to the distribution grid, compromising grid stability. This study applies machine learning algorithms to detect EV charging events within LV grids, to enhance load visibility for network planning. By analysing voltage fluctuations, current spikes, and power quality deviations, the research aims to identify potential overloads caused by EV charging. The study uses data collected over 25 weeks from three-phase transformers at an office area charging station. The outcome is expected to enhance grid resilience, mitigate equipment damage, and ensure the sustainable integration of EVs into LV grids, supporting network planners in grid upgrades and smart technology integration. Results demonstrate that EV charging events can be detected using a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) model with about 86% sensitivity and 78% specificity. Despite its proficiency in identifying EV charging events, the model seems to detect load fluctuations other than the EV-produced ones (false positives), evidencing the problem of load decoupling. Additionally, the presence of photovoltaic (PV) activity also seems to hinder model performance. Future efforts will focus on reducing false positives to improve EV detection performance and efficiently handle the presence of PV activity in the grid.

articleTitle: Hosting capacity in the Croatian regulatory environment
abstract: Installing distributed energy resources (DERs) in low voltage networks is limited by distribution grid codes, often defining a conservative connection power threshold, especially in the case of a single-phase connection or by the network’s technical constraints. Calculating the maximum installed power in that way is called hosting capacity (HC). Traditional HC calculation presents an assessment of static connection limits, determined by the lowest or highest electricity demand, depending on whether export or import limits are calculated. In this paper, we calculate the available range of aggregated active power of DERs based on worst-case and base-case demand scenarios. The results suggest the potential grid code redefinition since the analysed network can accommodate additional DERs in the range of 300 and 500 kW, compared to the current grid code limits. When observing only the grid code limitations in the import limits analysis, the results show an unrealistically high integration of more than 750 kW DERs, which is even higher than the best-case scenario. In the worst-case scenario, no additional DERs can be installed due to the initial violation of the network's constraints. Dynamic export and import limits are in the theoretical range of values, showing the benefit of the concept.

articleTitle: Strategic planning of an LVDC distribution network for the integration of EV charging stations
abstract: In an era defined by environmental consciousness and technological leaps, the electric vehicles market is undergoing unprecedented growth. Yet, this surge in power demand from electric vehicle charging stations puts into question the distribution network's capability to cater to the users’ needs. For this planning problem, there are two viable strategies: reinforcing the existing AC electrical infrastructure or implementing an innovative direct current distribution network. This paper explores the direct current paradigm, driven by the interest in its higher power transfer capability, reduced costs, and improved efficiency. In this context, a case study was defined: the design and sizing of a low voltage direct current (LVDC) distribution network to meet the additional power demand from electric vehicle charging stations in a workplace neighborhood. This work yielded a generalized algorithm that processes raw network data, checks current and voltage constraints, and then selects the optimal branch architecture. Simply put, this study showcases the potential of LVDC to address the evolving power demands and network planning challenges.

articleTitle: Modeling investment decisions of industrial prosumers in battery storage technologies considering STEEP factors
abstract: This paper investigates the investment behaviors of industrial prosumers in battery storage technologies, analyzing the influence of Social, Technological, Economic, Environmental, and Political factors from 2021 to 2030. The focus is on modeling how these factors affect the adoption of sodium-based and lithium iron phosphate battery technologies among European manufacturers. Employing the diffusion of innovations theory, we categorize industrial prosumers to predict their investment decisions in response to technological advances and market dynamics. The energy sector’s hosting hosting capacity and the integration of new technologies is respected by enhancing understanding and strategic planning among manufacturers, prosumers, and policymakers. Our findings suggest tailored market strategies that not only predict investment outcomes but also significantly enhance the industry’s view on existing and new technological solutions.

articleTitle: Using smart meter data to analyse low carbon technology loads in Northern Ireland
abstract: To achieve Northern Ireland’s decarbonisation objectives, a large volume of low carbon technology (LCT) loads are forecasted to connect at the edge of distribution networks. A lack of visibility of the low voltage network makes it difficult to investigate technical challenges such as network congestion, wider network imbalances, and sharper slopes towards peak demand. Low voltage monitoring and customer measurements are essential to forecast the effect of mass deployment on LCTs on the low voltage network to meet international and national commitments. Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) Networks strategically deployed 1, 000 smart meters in domestic customer premises as part of a 2022 pilot project. Approximately 70% of meters were installed at premises with an LCT such as a rooftop photovoltaic system, an electric vehicle or a heat pump. In this paper, half-hourly smart meter data is used to generate customer profiles. As expected, customers with LCT loads showed a significant increase in peak demand against non-LCT customers. The effect of time-of-use tariffs is also clear with some customers presenting overnight peak demands significantly higher than traditional tea time peaks. This is a fundamental shift in network investment drivers, network operation costs and potential generation triggers.

articleTitle: The impact of battery energy storage systems and their potential use as a flexibility in operational planning process
abstract: Stationary battery energy storage systems (BESS) at utility level are emerging as an attractive solution mainly due to the evolution of the technology and the definition of new energy and ancillary services. While BESS offer significant flexibility, their high power and capacity present challenges for distribution system operators in several processes such as the short-term operational planning. In the present paper, the impact of BESS in the short-term operational planning is analysed considering a real medium voltage distribution grid and realistic power consumption and generation scenarios. To perform this analysis a framework based in open-source tools was developed, including the power flow simulation and the operational planning algorithms. The first conclusion of the assessment is that BESS should be modelled in the operational planning process and new ways of representing the flexibility of BESS are needed. The concept of power operation enveloped has been tested showing the effectiveness of the method to addresses the challenges introduced by BESS.

articleTitle: Storage-driven business models: unlocking grid hosting capacity
abstract: The current regulatory framework states that DSOs shall not own, develop, manage, or operate energy storage facilities. However, using BESS can be a crucial enabler to promote the increase of hosting capacity. This paper addresses a possible concept project being designed by E-REDES where a BESS is installed in a primary substation to enable the connection of additional solar PV power plant on its network without impacting the TSO while promoting benefits for the whole electric system. Currently, in Portugal, BESS solutions are being developed as co-located (behind-the-meter) to hybridise power plants. For substation grids with a high density of solar PV power plants, DSO can promote a solution which allows the developer to have the opportunity to install a stand-alone BESS solution in those substations with pre-defined restrictions on discharge and/or obligation of charge energy in certain periods, particularly when strong solar production is expected. In this paper, the benefits and drawbacks of this solution are analysed from the point of view of the DSO while a grid services solution developer evaluates the business use case and possible revenue stacking opportunities to make this solution feasible from its standpoint.

articleTitle: Extension in load capacity thank to real-time monitoring of grid components
abstract: The energy transition from fossil fuels to sustainable energy sources and the increase of energy demand are putting the energy distribution grid under stress. Resilience in operations and reliability in asset protection are driving the transformation of the modern smart grid. Medium Voltage grid components are innovating, extending the traditional roles with additional functions to provide flexibility in operations and support the challenge of the electrifications. The ability to monitor the asset allows to optimize the component usage and extend temporary their operating area providing ‘load capacity’ flexibility such as during the peak power requests by the loads. The paper focused on medium voltage air insulated switchgears, as one of the larger grid components used in the power distribution system. Among the main indicators in the panels to monitor the operational conditions, thermal monitor of the main circuit conductors/bus bar appears as one of the most suitable to assess the impact on the equipment of the ‘load capacity extension’. The study presents a smart dynamic thermal monitoring method based on multiple data (currents, environmental and main circuit temperatures) and demonstrate how this approach can be used both to manage temporary overload of the circuit as well as to detect potential anomalous status of the equipment.

articleTitle: Assessing maximum grid loadability under PV deployment for distribution planning support: a Swiss case study
abstract: The increasing integration of low-carbon technologies, such as solar photovoltaics (PV) and heat pumps, impacts the operational margins of distribution grids. This paper quantifies the margins to voltage violation and line overloading by calculating the maximum grid loadability (MGL). We quantify this metric for 873 inferred Swiss medium-voltage grids and investigate the effect of rooftop PV and heat pump deployment by 2040. Results show a median MGL increase of 4.8% due to PV in summer and a median decrease of 11.1% due to heat pumps in winter. Overall, MGL is projected to increase by 14.0% until 2040, primarily driven by efficiency measures decreasing conventional loads. We highlight grid diversity, flexibility, energy efficiency, and winter peak as distribution planning considerations influencing operational margins.

articleTitle: Squeezing the hosting capacity: what is the value of active power curtailment?
abstract: The planning option of active power curtailment in electrical distribution grids intends to quickly integrate renewable energy sources into the grid, manage grid reinforcement and expansion, and prioritize planning measures. In Germany, a curtailment of 3 % of the annual production of photovoltaic plants and onshore wind power plants is allowed in the planning. Adequately representing these 3 % in grid planning is a challenge that has been addressed in several studies. There are a few caveats regarding the consideration of operational expenditures. On the one hand, the inconsistency between the “compliance with the 3 % criterion” in grid planning and operation makes it obsolete to derive the “real curtailed energy” (grid operation) within the planning process. On the other hand, there is a lack of dependable price assumptions for the reimbursement of the curtailed energy. In this paper, we show how different assumptions for the criterion compliance and the curtailment price change the economic effect of curtailment. To this end, we propose a framework for the assessment of criterion compliance and conduct a case study on a German MV grid model.

articleTitle: Protection of new MV networks
abstract: This paper describes the problems presented by overcurrent protection in meshed distribution networks and the advantages provided by distance and line differential protection. It also explains the difficulties that these latter protections have and the solutions applied. Results from RTDS simulations of a MV line are included.

articleTitle: Grid-aware demand response in energy communities
abstract: To tackle climate change, large amounts of distributed renewable power generation capacities will be installed over the coming years. At the same time, the electrification of the mobility and heating sectors will increase the amount of flexible loads connected to power grids. Energy communities can promote an increased consumption of locally generated renewable power by providing price incentives for community participants. Therefore, energy communities could help reduce the strain on distribution grids from increased distributed power generation and further electrification of energy consumption. We present a co-simulation approach for energy communities and respective grid infrastructure. Employing this co-simulation approach we evaluate different heuristic control algorithms and their effect on the power distribution grid. Communicating grid congestion to community members can help reduce negative effects on power grids. In the realistic scenarios we present, the flexibility offered by energy communities is not sufficient to avert negative effects completely.

articleTitle: E-REDES pioneer solution for DSO observability and control to manage client-side flexibility
abstract: The energy transition and the increased electrification of our society requires the DSO (Distribution System Operator) implementation of advanced monitoring and control systems to ensure grid safety, stability and reliability. DSOs are increasingly incentivised to conduct flexible grid management to increase DER (Distributed Energy Resources) integration with minimal infrastructure increase. However, this entails the need for observability and control of generation stations, prosumers and, in some cases, consumption clients. The Portuguese DSO, E-REDES, identified the necessity of expanding the flexibility on the HV (High Voltage) and MV (Medium Voltage) grid operation by enhancing the observability and control of the connection points to such clients. Considering this need, a proposal was put forward for developing a multipurpose, economically viable and standard device to be integrated into the interconnection point between the distribution grid and the customer's grid of all types of clients connected to the HV and MV. This paper details the proposed innovative architecture scheme and possible use cases. The authors believe this approach constitutes an economical solution where synergies with metering are used to provide real-time observability and control that can be used to manage flexibility, leveraging the implementation and usage of an Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS).

articleTitle: Dynamic thermal loading capacity of underground cables in medium voltage distribution networks
abstract: Rapid advancement of technology and the inclusion of newer technologies in the medium voltage (MV) distribution grid has a negative effect on its hosting capacity. A complete restructure of the existing grid infrastructure is not a viable option owing to the economic as well as practical reasons. To counter this, an approach is proposed in this paper to increase the hosting capacity of the grid via better utilization of its underground cables. A comparison between the static approach which is based on the nominal current of the cable and the dynamic approach based on the temperature properties to determine the load rate is done. The results from this study show that there is indeed more room available as even though the nominal current of the cable is reached, the component is sufficiently below the safety threshold recommended based on its heating. This implies that the grid has more space to accommodate new consumers as well as Distribution Energy Resources (DERs). A brief insight into the methodology followed by the initial results based on this approach and further steps to be taken are explained in this paper.

articleTitle: Optimizing smart grid hosting capacity: lessons from IEC 61850 substation maintenance and documentation validation
abstract: The concept of network hosting capacity is closely tied to the broader idea of the smart grid. According to IEC, the IEC 61850 standard is a core standard of the smart grid. In this context, IEC 61850 substations serve as crucial reference points for the entire smart grid system. The strength of IEC 61850 lies in its modelling capabilities, providing a future-proof aspect that extends beyond communication protocols. It establishes the groundwork for standardized documentation of substations, facilitating easy interfacing with other entities in the power system in the future, such as, but not limited to, storage systems. In line with this vision, a Swedish DSO collaborated with an IEC 61850 testing company to conduct a maintenance project to validate the accuracy of the IEC 61850 documentation (SCD files), for their substations. The tests have been carried out while the substations were in operation. The insights gained have far-reaching implications for the coming engineering of IEC 61850 substations, the importance of SCD documentation to facilitate maintenance and upgrades or modifications. The study also highlights the importance of "substation testability" during operation, the necessity for further advancing "non- intrusive testing methods," and the need to integrate testing considerations into the initial engineering phases. The hosting capacity of the network comes with a cost, and any effort to reduce this cost at engineering and maintenance activities, represents a significant contribution to the overall penetration of the smart grid in all the voltage levels.

articleTitle: Reliable and secure control center to station device communication
abstract: The increasing demands on the power grid require intelligent and flexible solutions that ensure the grid’s stability. Many of these measures involve sophisticated communication between the control center and the stations that is not efficiently realizable using traditional protocols, e.g., IEC 60870-5-104. To this end, IEC 61850 introduces data models which allow flexible communication. Still, the specification leaves open how DSOs should interconnect their stations to realize resilient communication between the control center and station devices. However, DSOs require such communication to adapt modern solutions increasing the grid’s capacity, e.g., adaptive protection systems. In this paper, we present our envisioned network and communication concept for future DSO’s ICT infrastructures that enables the control center to resiliently and flexibly communicate with station devices. For resilience, we suggest interconnecting each station with two distinct communication paths to the control center, use MPLS-TP and MPTCP for fast failovers when a single link fails, and mTLS to protect the communication possibilities against misuse. Additionally, in accordance with IEC 61850, we envision the control center to communicate with the station devices using MMS by using the station RTU as a proxy.

articleTitle: Distribution network voltage forecasting based on graph convolutional networks – long short-term memory
abstract: The integration of renewable energy sources increases the complexity of distribution systems and the uncertainty of node voltages, thereby amplifying the importance of precise voltage forecasting to maintain system stability. Voltage forecasting is traditionally performed using mathematical models. However, these models have limitations in analysing the diversity of loads and the overvoltage and congestion caused by renewable energy outputs. Thus, AI-based voltage forecasting using data-based approaches is being widely studied to refine forecasting models based on bus to account for temporal voltage variability. However, the voltage of a bus is closely related to those of adjacent buses, necessitating their consideration in forecasting models. In this paper, a graph convolutional networks–long short-term memory-based forecasting model is developed that considers the interconnection information between buses to determine the characteristics of adjacent buses in the distribution system. The proposed method has been validated via simulations.

articleTitle: Improving distribution system state estimation: novel metadata driven approach for pseudo measurement generation
abstract: As the shift towards renewable energy progresses, the importance of accurately monitoring the distribution grid increases. Traditional monitoring has been challenged by the sparse deployment of measuring devices across medium and low voltage grids. This research introduces two novel AI-based approaches to generate realistic pseudo measurements (PMs) for medium-voltage busbars, utilizing consumer structure metadata and historical data. When these PMs are applied to estimate bus voltages in the medium-voltage grid, their accuracy proves comparable to that of historical measurements. However, in predicting line loadings, a forecasting error increase of up to 60 % is observed, though the prediction of critical line segments remains reliable using PMs alone. This study not only highlights the potential of PMs in enhancing grid monitoring but also suggests an optimized strategy for placing measuring devices to achieve the most accurate state estimation results.

articleTitle: Enabling the future: digitalizing low voltage networks and enhancing hosting capacity through digital twin
abstract: In an era marked by significant technological progress, the digitalization of Low Voltage (LV) networks emerges as a pivotal component in controlling and operating energy distribution systems. This paper underscores the importance of digitalization in integrating Distributed Energy Resources (DERs), Electric Vehicles (EVs), and Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems into LV networks. It outlines the essential steps and challenges in creating a digital twin of the LV network, which is crucial for enhancing the network's capacity and ensuring the quality of electrical supply at minimal cost. This process involves three critical phases: mapping the network topology and cable traces using Geographic Information System (GIS) technologies, monitoring the LV distribution network through advanced devices, and employing a Power Flow Simulation (PFS) tool to find congestion points accurately. The paper highlights the importance of each step to develop a resilient LV network. It emphasizes the need for accurate network topology databases, real-time data collection, and the application of PFS tools based on error-free network mapping and smart meter data. In conclusion, digitalization holds the key to optimize grid capacity and accommodate a greater number of DERs, EVs, and HVAC systems, provided distribution companies can accurately model their physical networks.

articleTitle: Recursive hosting capacity region assessment to further unleash grid power potential
abstract: Evolving from the notion of "hosting capacity", hosting capacity region defines a combined feasible region in the operational space given by various installations in radial grids. Within the region, all operation points adhere to power flow outcomes that meet the criteria for grid voltage and current limitations. By synchronizing operations among these installations, this region helps to fully unleash the grid power potential. Enlightened by computational geometry, the region can be quickly assessed by computing an asymptotic convex polytope, while with inherent accuracy loss due to the necessity for an inner approximation. To enhance the region approximation accuracy, this paper introduces a recursive assessment approach, where the current-related elements in the exact grid model will be refined iteratively. Unlike the conventional approach of relaxing the cable current to its nominal threshold, the iterations aim to suppress such upper bound by calculating maximal cable current of all extreme points within the previously assessed region. This generates a grid model with stricter relaxation, eventually contributing to higher region accuracy. Case studies implemented on a 10.5 kV Dutch grid model have confirmed the efficacy of the proposed scheme, which reduces 23.29% assessment accuracy loss compared to the state-of-art scheme in current literature.

articleTitle: Key takeaways and hands-on experiences with the introduction of a local flexibility market implementation at E.ON Hungary
abstract: There are many pilot projects around Europe with the scope of flexibility. The Flex.on program is a Hungarian program led by E.ON which conceptualized and implemented a comprehensive flexibility platform. The platform covers all DSO voltage levels with particular challenges. Several Local Flexibility Platforms are developing in Europe, but there is no seen such wide scope in terms of voltage levels that Flex.on flexibility platform brought into focus. This ambitious goal meant that significant challenges had to be faced both in terms of research questions and IT development. In this paper we showcase only an LV scenario in detail due to the lack of space, although the platform handles all voltage levels in a similar manner.

articleTitle: Making hosting capacity estimates more reliable through automated GIS corrections
abstract: The energy transition is having a major impact on the operation and planning of low voltage distribution networks. Uncertainties in network length, topology or number and type of customers can lead to sub-optimal investment decisions. This work aims to enhance the reliability of hosting capacity estimates, enabling better decisions on network reinforcement. A combination of smart meter data, open data address repositories and network cartography is used to automatically detect and correct GIS anomalies.

articleTitle: The distribution electricity grid: new challenges and risks
abstract: The distribution grid is expected to undergo annual demand and capacity changes in the current uncertain market. Using data from the Portuguese DSO, the paper found a 57% peak demand index in primary substations and a 40% capacity availability for both standardized and non-standardized substations. Despite projections showing the grid can handle current energy demands, especially from the transportation sector, there are looming challenges ahead. Due to policy changes, increasing EV adoption, and the rise of prosumers, constant monitoring of grid capacity in primary and secondary substations is crucial. The paper also suggests strategies like traditional investments, load management, and a new self-consumption paradigm in Portugal as a non-traditional tool.

articleTitle: DC power quality analysis: technical insights for LVDC networks and measurement systems
abstract: The adoption of DC grids in distribution networks is on the rise and is anticipated to gain further prominence in the coming years owing to several benefits compared to conventional AC systems. Nonetheless, the integration of DC in the electric grid faces many obstacles and challenges to guarantee its effective implementation. Some of these obstacles can be listed as follows: the lack of standards for the assessment of Power Quality in DC grids (DCPQ), which includes voltage and current ripples, transients, spectral components, etc., the recommendation of DCPQ indices to characterise these disturbances and the definition of measurement techniques for DC grids. Therefore, this paper aims to address these challenges by conducting a comprehensive literature review and analysing measurements obtained from a LVDC prototype developed in China.

articleTitle: Increasing the RES hosting capacity of the Cyprus distribution system
abstract: The Renewable Energy Sources (RES) penetration in the power system of Cyprus has dramatically increased over the last years. As a result, the system is already facing significant challenges limiting the RES hosting capacity of the Distribution Network (DN). The major limitation factors are network congestion and voltage security. In this paper, alternative solutions for increasing the RES hosting capacity in DNs are reviewed, and a methodology is introduced to evaluate their effectiveness. More specifically, different inverter settings and an advanced centralised voltage control from power transformers are used to mitigate voltage-related issues, while network reinforcements and upgrading the operating voltage are considered for further increase in hosting capacity. The solutions and evaluation methodology are tested using a real MV network of the Cyprus distribution system and the strategic plan of the Cyprus Distribution System Operator (DSO) for maximizing RES hosting capacity is outlined.

articleTitle: Increasing low voltage grid hosting capacity for production by active power flexibility: cost-benefit analysis and sensitivity study
abstract: In the baseline scenario of its “Plan de développement de reseau” (network development plan), ENEDIS (France's main DSO) expects to host 70GW of renewable energy in 2032, compared with around 28GW today. Substantial investment will be needed to support this scenario, while maintaining a secure and efficient power grid. To limit some of these investments or spread them over time, flexibilities can be used in certain situations. In the first part of this paper, we present an approach aimed at identifying situations where power curtailment on a specific low voltage grid may present an economic interest for the community. It highlights the key parameters which influence the benefits of this flexibility and concludes that it should be assessed on a case-by-case basis. In the second part, we look at the potential gain in terms of additional hosting capacity that a connection with power curtailment can bring compared with a conventional connection. In this stage, no constraints are authorized on the grid, i.e. no reinforcement would be needed to connect the producer. The gain in hosting capacity is presented in the form of a map.

articleTitle: Embedding operating envelopes in the market design to unlock the flexibility potential of distribution grids
abstract: The increased need for flexibility by transmission system operators requires an increase in participation of distributed flexibility. However, this participation must concurrently ensure the operational security of the distribution grids, so as not to violate distribution system operational constraints through transmission-level flexibility activations. Towards this end, this paper studies the operating envelope (OE) approach for dynamically including distribution system constraints in transmission system flexibility markets. The paper considers three OE grouping levels (i.e., system level, flexibility provider level, or resource level) and different network models (i.e., power transfer distribution factors, LinDistFlow, and second-order cone programming formulations) for the calculation of the OEs. The approach is then benchmarked against the market formulations with full inclusion of network constraints. A case study analysis showcases that these OE network abstraction methods can be used to promote the utilization of distributed flexibility in a secure manner. However, their application differs in terms of grid-safety guarantees, resulting impact on market efficiency, and the volume of constrained flexibility imposed by the grid limits.

articleTitle: The impact of a battery energy storage system in Terceira Island, Azores
abstract: This article presents the early results and impact of a Battery Energy Storage System in Terceira's electric grid.

articleTitle: Towards a more efficient congestion management for the transformation of electric distribution grids with increasing share of sector-coupled components
abstract: The increasing acceleration of the energy transition is leading to major changes in the entire energy system. Not only are conventional energy generation plants increasingly being replaced by decentralized renewable generators with the aim of decarbonization, but the heating and mobility sectors are also being electrified at a rapid pace. A large share of this transformation is taking place in the distribution grids, especially in low-voltage grids, which are likely to be exposed to grid congestions as a result. In Germany the legislation has decided to support distribution grid operators by the adjustment of the German Energy Act. Controllable consumption units, for example electric heat pumps and non-public loading infrastructure of electric vehicles, have to adjust their consumption in grid congestion situations according to the requirements. This will solve some of the problem situations, but further aids are needed. In this paper two different grid congestion management strategies based on the current legal framework are investigated. The default strategy is handling the congestions by means of current- and voltage-based congestion indicators, the new strategy uses an approach based on the cable temperature. The results show, that even in disadvantageous installation conditions the transient thermal behaviour offers flexibility for congestion management.

articleTitle: Constraint enforcing for learning the ACOPF using neural networks
abstract: This paper explores the application of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to solving the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) task. While numerical optimisation techniques have been widely used, their computational complexity limits their real-world applicability. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), in particular the use of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), offer promising avenues to overcome these limitations. In this effort, we explore the incorporation of the OPF inequality constraints into the architecture of the DNN using activation functions such as clipping, and shifted and scaled sigmoid. Supervised training of the developed models on synthetic datasets demonstrates that the constraints can be enforced at no additional cost, thereby improving prediction accuracy and providing significant speedup compared to the Interior Point Optimiser (IPOPT).

articleTitle: Dynamic DSO network development and planning - integrated decision support in the face of uncertainty
abstract: The energy transition of the power, heat and transport systems is taking place in the electrical distribution grids, which poses major challenges for all distribution system operators. Large parts of the infrastructure must be expanded, optimized and digitized quickly and cost-effectively. Classic, mostly manual network planning procedures are reaching their limits with respect to processing times and complexity. Therefore, a central and automated approach was developed that carries out a holistic and multifactorial analysis of all networks. This means that a complete set of needed action is determined, including hotspots due to excessive load flow, age- and condition-related renewal requirements, reliability, and a predefined digitization strategy. Based on the existing and expected need for action, an expansion path emerges that on the one hand provides the right measures at the right time and, on the other hand, compiles and prioritizes them in such a way that as many problems as possible are solved at once or avoided before they would even occur. Time and money are saved and are available for an even faster and more targeted expansion of the networks. In concrete terms, this means more connection capacity in a shorter time at lower costs.

articleTitle: Impact of unmanaged PV development on hosting capacity in coupled MV-LV distribution networks
abstract: Distributed PV generation is an increasingly popular way of integrating renewable energy sources into the power system. High PV penetration can, however, lead to issues, particularly overvoltage in LV networks. To accurately evaluate when issues can occur, interactions between LV and MV networks must be considered, as the LV hosting capacity can be reduced by PV development in other parts of the network. This paper presents a coupled MV-LV model to study the interactions between networks with a high amount of PV generation. The MV-LV transformers are modelled with tap changers, further limiting the available PV hosting capacity, as tap positions are set to avoid undervoltage in winter. Hosting capacity is determined stochastically through Monte Carlo simulations of PV development, with results highlighting how PV systems affect voltages in neighbouring LV networks. LV networks with high transformer tap positions are particularly vulnerable to overvoltage and reduce the expected hosting capacity of the distribution network as a whole. In addition, a simple heuristic limiting PV penetration in each LV network based on tap position is implemented, improving the expected MV network’s PV hosting capacity by 250%, and reducing variance. This indicates a possible socio-economic utility of managing distributed PV development, through curtailment or other means.

articleTitle: Decarbonisation demands decentralisation: how blockchain is impacting the energy sector
abstract: In the transition to a society with net-zero carbon emissions, high penetration of renewable energy sources and novel energy vectors are driving traditional operational systems, models, and processes towards emerging digital solutions that facilitate the changes occurring in the energy sector. As a radical shift to decentralisation and digitalisation unfolds, blockchain technology emerges as a key enabler of this transformation. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the evolving role and potential of blockchain in supporting the energy sector's move to a more sustainable, efficient, and transparent system. Through the lens of blockchain’s capabilities, this paper explores how this technology can address the challenges of a rapidly digitalising energy landscape and offer a strategic advantage in the transition to a net-zero future. Specifically, blockchain facilitates increased hosting capacity by enabling dynamic interactions between distributed energy resources and the grid, ensuring real-time management and optimisation. This capability directly supports the grid in accommodating larger volumes of renewable sources without the need for extensive physical upgrades.

articleTitle: A hybrid model for the participation of water heaters in new complex demand response policies
abstract: The participation of residential segments in electricity markets face to multitude of barriers. For instance, a minimum flexibility threshold level, achievable through aggregation, is required. These aggregation processes make more complex and slower the evaluation of response which can be a technical problem to respond to some services, for instance, ancillary services, and can get more and more complexity if a customer group is involved in several services. Thus, the aggregation process first requires the development of coherent load groups and then the simulation through elemental and aggregated models. The participation of groups of flexible loads in several markets and services presents an opportunity to achieve a greater revenue for the demand-side actors, the opportunity to share the cost of enabling technologies, that decreases customers engagement in DR, and the increase of the flexibility and capacity of networks. The proposal of this work is a platform that uses a physical-based hybrid model that suffers a segregation and a reduction of the model complexity to get an increase in the computational speed but considering the main physical phenomena to balance errors and the time of response.

articleTitle: Research and application of Koopman-based local voltage control of DG in distribution network
abstract: Due to the inherent volatility and intermittency, the output of the distributed generator (DG) fluctuates dramatically. The high penetration of DGs deteriorates the condition of voltage excursion in distribution networks. The model-based methods rely on accurate network parameters, which may be difficult to be applied in the practical operation. In contrast, data-driven-based methods can extract the operating rules of distribution networks with the operational data. In this paper, a data-driven-based voltage regulation method for DGs is proposed based on the Koopman theory. Training with the historical data, a control strategy generation model is established day-ahead, which reflects the complex relationship between states and strategies. Then, the model is decomposed into several sub-models and released to each local area. In the local stage, the sub-model can determine the control strategies of DGs during real-time operation by collecting local measurements and forecasting data. The proposed Koopman-based method can effectively alleviate the computational burden while achieving near-global optimization. It is beneficial to tackle the uncertainties of voltage fluctuations caused by DGs in distribution networks.

articleTitle: A dynamic method of assessing potential distribution network policy breaches due to localised load reduction flexibility service under varying levels of generation
abstract: The Network System Services (NSS) group in ESB Engineering and Major Projects (EMP) has been requested by the Power Systems Requirements (PSR) group in ESB Networks (ESBN) to conduct a review of the DSU (Demand Side Unit) demand reduction studies previously performed by ESBN. The review was conducted as part of the National Networks Local Connection Programme (NNLCP). During the rare scenario where you have maximum generation and summer valley load on a localized section of network, and then further reduce the load with demand reductions, localized violations of the distribution system’s operational limits may occur. This scenario has previously been studied within ESBN, with 14.6 MW of demand reduction customers being red-listed during the summer months in 2022 (April – September). The ask of NSS group was to reassess customers who were previously refused to determine if the network can host their demand reduction services under lower levels of generation.

articleTitle: Preventing congestion management by modelling cable temperatures: a real-world case
abstract: We show for a real-world grid connection containing solar and wind generation that congestion management can be prevented by using dynamic modelling of cable temperatures. Despite the fact that peak currents exceed the rated current of the cable, the cable temperature stays within the safe operating range. We apply Monte Carlo sampling on critical input parameters of the soil and cable positions to quantify the reliability of our model prediction under unavoidable input parameter uncertainty. We conclude with a discussion on how to implement this approach in congestion management systems and discuss further research.

articleTitle: Evaluating the trade-off between grid expansion and flexibility usage in electrical distribution grids
abstract: The increase of operational flexibility potential, provided by distributed energy resources (DER), might extend the distribution grid operators toolbox for congestion management beyond typically used measures such as grid expansion. However, the usage of grid expansion and flexibility measures are interdependent and their cost-minimal mix is unknown. Therefore, within the presented work, the trade-off between grid expansion and flexibility usage is investigated for three different coherent medium- and low-voltage grid structures. To evaluate the different degrees of grid expansion, multiple expansion variants are determined varying regarding their remaining thermal congestions. Subsequently, the optimal usage of flexibility to mitigate these remaining congestions is identified and the incurred costs are calculated. The investigations show that a sensible combination of both measures leads to cost optimal results. However, the optimal trade-off between grid expansion and flexibility usage is highly dependent on the grid structure. Within the rural grid, grid expansion measures can reduce the total costs by almost 80 %, whereas the usage of flexibility can reduce the total costs within the urban grid by 52 %.

articleTitle: Impact of dynamic operating envelopes on distribution network hosting capacity for electric vehicles
abstract: The examination of the maximum number of electric vehicles (EVs) that can be integrated into the distribution network (DN) without causing any operational incidents has become increasingly crucial as EV penetration rises. This issue can be addressed by utilizing dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs), which are generated based on the grid status. While DOEs improve the hosting capacity of the DN for EVs (EV-HC) by restricting the operational parameters of the network, they also alter the amount of energy needed for charging each EV, resulting in a decrease in the quality of service (QoS). This study proposes a network-aware hosting capacity framework for EVs (EV-NAHC) that i) aims to assess the effects of DOEs on active distribution networks, ii) introduces a novel definition for HC and calculates the EV-NAHC based on the aggregated QoS of all customers. A small-scale Belgian feeder is utilized to examine the proposed framework. The results show a substantial increase in the EV-NAHC with low, medium, and high-daily charging energy scenarios.

articleTitle: Community DSO: a community-led approach to smart local energy systems
abstract: Energy communities offer opportunities for customers to increase the value of system decentralisation, however they can be complex to establish and need to align with network needs for broader system benefit. Alongside this, the rapid deployment of low carbon technologies (LCTs) presents a challenge for network companies in operating and balancing electricity networks. The Community Distribution System Operator (Community DSO) concept proposes a solution to this complexity by engaging with LCTs within energy community “cells”. Each cell, based around a physical section of the network, manages loads at a local level. Community DSO could therefore create mutual value for both distribution network operators (DNOs) and the communities connected to their low voltage (LV) networks. For communities, this value is likely to be indirect, and could be very significant. For example, Community DSO might be a key enabler of local decarbonisation. The direct value to the DNO will be created through deferring and even avoiding the need for LV network reinforcement. Community DSO seeks to maximise this by encouraging high levels of participation in local flexibility that benefits both the network and community.

articleTitle: User survey on V2G and V2H acceptance – motivators and future implications
abstract: Bidirectional charging of electric vehicles (EVs) can play an important role in balancing electricity supply and demand in future electric energy system and improve the hosting capacity of EVs and renewable energy resources. However, since the main purpose of the EVs is to provide transportation instead of grid services, it is of crucial importance to consider EV users’ perspective when designing approaches for sustainable EV-grid integration. To this end, EV users’ attitudes towards bidirectional charging was investigated using a survey. The results show that, despite the concerns seen in vehicle-to-grid and vehicle-to-home, there is hope for large scale adoption of such technology.

articleTitle: Towards digitalized and automated substations: implementation of adaptive protection control unit and monitoring system for modern distribution networks under increased hosting capacity of distributed renewable sources
abstract: Maximizing the hosting capacity of modern distribution networks to accommodate more distributed renewable sources is key driver to realise energy system security and Net-Zero carbon goals. Protection systems under increased share of renewable sources became more challenging with diverse topology changes originated from the addition, disconnection, or islanding of distributed generation to secure increasing energy demands. This paper aims to implement an adaptive protection control unit interlinked with an interactive monitoring system to enable the real-world application of smart adaptive protection schemes for modern distribution networks under increased hosting capacity of distributed renewable sources. An adaptive protection control kit is experimentally developed to enable the automatic adjustment of optimal relay settings in response to network topology changes arising from the integration of distributed generation. A set of relay settings are pre-optimized within a small-scale meshed network under possible network topologies and stored offline via a master microcontroller which then uses the online breaker status to identify the corresponding network topology and accordingly adjust the pre-optimized relay settings. A human machine interface is further designed and interlinked with the experimentally developed control kit via a slave microcontroller, providing real-time data of actual current measurements and waveforms together with topological changes and self-adaptation of pre-optimized relay settings. Experimental results showed successful adjustment of pre-optimized relay settings in response to topological changes while achieving coordination time intervals within acceptable limits under the tested network topologies.

articleTitle: Operational planning in distribution control centres for enhancing hosting capacity
abstract: Amidst evolving energy landscapes, Distribution System Operators (DSOs) navigate a dynamic terrain shaped by emerging technologies and increased distributed energy resource (DER) integration. This paper explores the paradigm shift from passive to active DER management, highlighting the evolution of Distribution Control Centres (DCC) and the emergence of distribution operational planning. Dynamic Operating Envelopes (DOE) are envisioned as a transformative concept to optimize DER usage within grid limits. Factors influencing DOE development, such as grid visibility and analytical methods, are analysed, emphasizing their role in comprehensive resource management. Key objectives include evolving the role of distribution operational planning, elucidating DOE dynamics, and highlighting its strategic importance amidst evolving distribution systems. The paper also underscores the criticality of strategic planning as utilities deploy advanced systems like distribution automation and DER management.

articleTitle: Techno-economic analysis of single-phase, versus three-phase load dependant, dynamic set-point control in voltage regulating distribution transformers (VRDT) to increase hosting capacity of low voltage networks
abstract: The increased installation of distributed energy resources (DER), heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers forces distribution system operators (DSO) to increase the hosting capacity of their grids. Voltage regulating distribution transformers (VRDT) are a proven asset to tackle this goal. These on-load tap-changer (OLTC) equipped distribution transformers allow automatic voltage regulation at the low voltage bus bar. Thus, VRDTs decouple low voltage networks from the upstream medium voltage variations and allow a broader voltage band for both, generation, and load situation and therefore increasing hosting capacity. This contribution describes different voltage control algorithms, the implications to hosting capacity enhancement, networks planning aspects, and the decision process of the Dutch DSO Alliander’s decision to choose dynamic set-point control as their standard for VRDTs. The set-up of the technology used is a three-phase measurement unit. A techno economic project evaluation of a dynamic voltage regulation with single-phase measurement against the established three-phase arrangement is undertaken. As a result, the decision was made to develop and introduce single-phase dynamic set-point control in VRDTs, due to the advantage of reduced purchasing cost, reduced space requirements and usage of resources, minimised installation and commissioning effort, that outweigh the disadvantages caused by the reduced measurement set-up.

articleTitle: Study on hosting capacity criteria other than thermal capacity in distribution network using long-term and geospatial load forecast
abstract: In Japan, further expansion of photovoltaic (PV) installation is expected toward carbon neutrality by 2050. To determine the amount of PV that can be added to distribution system without countermeasures, or hosting capacity (HC), the Kansai Transmission and Distribution, Inc. mainly uses the current value; however, voltage violations could occur without overloads. Therefore, this study examined whether voltage violations should be considered as HC criteria in addition to thermal capacity. First, long-term and geospatial load forecasts were conducted for 3,451 distribution lines in Hyogo Prefecture. Second, actual measurements were conducted on the distribution line selected using the load forecasts and specifications of the distribution lines, showing voltage drops due to reactance with the long distribution line and reactive power from PV inverter with fixed power factor. Third, we performed simulation of countermeasures for the voltage violations in the distribution line by power flow analysis and discussed the availability of the long-term and geospatial forecasts in distribution grid planning. Lastly, we estimated that 527 distribution lines would have zero HC by 2050 without countermeasures using the load forecasts. The fact that 25% of them were caused by lower voltage limits indicated its importance as HC criteria in Japan.

articleTitle: Using state estimation voltage limitation as indicator for renewable generation curtailment
abstract: High levels of renewable generation can lead to temporarily voltage issues, particularly since the distribution network was not initially designed to handle large amounts of fluctuating and intermittent renewable energy generation. For short-term periods, curtailing renewable generation may be necessary to prevent voltage violations. State estimation is used to estimate the current state of the distribution network, including voltages, powers and loading at all nodes. It considers measurements from various operational and measurement devices to estimate the state variables of the system. Voltage limitation state estimation specifically focuses on identifying and addressing voltage-related issues and notifying the distribution network operator of such violations. This paper is focused on using voltage limitation state estimation as an indicator for renewable generation curtailment. Parallel calculations processes that recognize when voltage limits are being approached or violated will be examined in order to better understand the validity and the trueness of the triggers that can then initiate further curtailment measures. The case study is focused on state estimation data in relation to voltage violation of the voltage limits and the comparison to smart-meter derived voltages to check the correctness of the estimated voltage state at LV service locations. Curtailment measures can then be considered as a point to conditionally approve and increase more renewable generation integration in distribution network.

articleTitle: Application of operating envelopes to increase hosting capacity for smart charging facilities in urban distribution grids
abstract: The present work explores the application of operating envelopes to increase hosting capacity for smart charging facilities in urban distribution grids. The concept of an operating envelope, which is a dynamic active power limit provided by distribution system operators (DSO) via a bi-directional DSO-to-customer interface, is analysed using the example of a parking garage with an intelligent smart charging hub. The study shows that compared to static limits, introducing dynamic operating envelopes significantly reduce violations in number and extent while increasing hosting capacity for additional charging stations for electric mobility. Further research is planned to evaluate the impact on transformer limits and further develop the DER-Interaction-Module (Distributed Energy Resources) as a DSO-to-customer interface.

articleTitle: Effects of negative spot market prices on electricity distribution network loading, experiences from the Finnish distribution system
abstract: On November 24th, an extreme case occurred in the Nordic electricity market, especially in the Finnish market area, when spot prices for half a day reached values of -500 €/MWh. This meant that even with distribution fees and taxes added to the spot price, end-users were still paid over 0.4 €/kWh for electrical energy use, providing a high incentive for electricity end-users to consume electricity. Statistics show that consumption increased considerably as the spot prices declined. The main increase in consumption was in the households having spot-price-based electricity retail contracts that provided a direct incentive to increase electricity consumption. Because of increased loads, a considerable number of load points’ fuses melted and even some network fuses melted.

articleTitle: NIE networks low voltage optimisation through active network management
abstract: This paper presents findings from trials investigating the implementation of Low Voltage Active Network Management (LV ANM) schemes within Northern Ireland Electricity Networks' licence area. The study evaluates the impact of strategic network reconfiguration, including the closure of normally open positions and the establishment of meshed networks, on voltage and power dynamics. Results demonstrate notable improvements in voltage levels and daily peak power reduction throughout the tested LV networks, addressing issues commonly associated with increased renewable energy integration. Moreover, positive changes in active power within the LV network highlight enhanced visibility, control, and optimisation capabilities afforded by LV ANM. Reconfiguration of feeder networks facilitated more efficient utilisation of available capacity, thereby reducing peak loading of assets. Additionally, the implementation of LV ANM could contribute to deferring network reinforcement costs, showcasing the economic benefits of this approach. These findings underscore the case for integration of LV ANM into regular operations, offering tangible benefits for modern power distribution systems in terms of reliability, efficiency, and sustainability.

articleTitle: Increasing DER hosting capacity in Öland, Sweden, via active network management (ANM)
abstract: The Öland distribution network in Sweden has experienced generation development to a degree where any further generation connections will exceed network capacity limits. Under traditional network design principles, new hosting capacity must be provided by adding capacity through building new assets or reinforcing existing assets. This traditional approach requires expensive replacement or addition of grid infrastructure, and will provide grid capacity that is only required under very rare extreme operating conditions on the network. As an alternative to grid reinforcement, E.ON is introducingnon-firmcurtailable network connections to increase grid hosting capacity without the need for grid reinforcement. E.ON is demonstrating the granular curtailment of generator export under these extreme network conditions, achieved via Active Network Management (ANM) technology. This approach avoids costly reinforcement of the network across Öland and presents lower-cost and accelerated connection for the renewable generators connecting to the distribution network. This paper presents the hosting capacity challenge at Öland, representative of challenges faced across the distribution network in Sweden. The ANM functions are described alongside integration of DLR, reactive power management and the inter-relation between the different solutions. The paper shares the learning from the implementation of the solution.

articleTitle: Harmonic-aware hosting capacity assessment for ultrafast EV charging stations: a Dutch MV grid case study
abstract: Ultrafast electric vehicle (EV) charging stations are essential for mitigating range anxiety and facilitating smooth mobility transition. To obey rigorous grid power quality standards, the harmonic emissions of ultrafast charging stations should be included when the distribution system operators (DSOs) determine their hosting capacity, particularly considering their cumulative grid impacts as power levels increase. For computation burden reduction, a voltage-dependent harmonic current estimator will replace the complicated power electronics model. This estimator is integrated into the load flow model to assess the grid harmonic impacts from respective charging stations. By iterative calculations until convergence, those harmonic impacts can be answered in a numerical manner, thus enabling harmonic-aware hosting capacity assessment. An examination of a real-world 298-bus 10.5 kV grid in the Netherlands highlighted the necessity of harmonic awareness during hosting capacity assessment, especially in the scenario of high network background harmonics.
